abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a rare disorder with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 50,000. Management of HAE brings challenges including the frequency of delivery of the medication, routes of medication delivery, cost of treatment and significant impact on quality of life for patients with HAE. Donidalorsen is the newest FDA-approved long-term prophylaxis medication for HAE that offers substantial benefits over its competitors.
AREAS COVERED: A search of the current literature on donidalorsen was conducted using the PubMed and Cochrane libraries. In this review, we discuss the mechanism and clinical efficacy of donidalorsen. We also explore the comparison between donidalorsen and other agents on the market for the long-term prophylaxis of HAE. The safety profile of donidalorsen as well as a discussion on the economic impact of donidalorsen is also reviewed.
EXPERT OPINION: Donidalorsen offers a promising option for treatment of HAE, with substantial attack reduction, infrequent dosing, and improved quality of life. Continued long-term safety data are needed, but donidalorsen may become a leading prophylactic option for HAE worldwide.

abstract: Ovarian cancer remains one of the most lethal gynecological malignancies, largely due to late diagnosis and the frequent development of resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy and taxanes. Increasing evidence implicates microRNAs as key regulators of drug response through their control of DNA damage response and repair, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and therapy-induced cellular senescence. Senescence is a double-edged process characterized by irreversible cell-cycle arrest and the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, which may suppress tumor growth but also promote chemoresistance and disease recurrence. This review summarizes current evidence on microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulation of therapy-induced cellular senescence and its role in drug resistance in ovarian cancer. We integrate data from mechanistic studies, preclinical models, and clinical observations, focusing on senescence-associated miRNAs and their regulatory networks. miRNAs including miR-34a, miR-21, miR-146a, miR-200c, miR-506, and miR-433 regulate key senescence pathways, notably p53/p21 and p16-RB signaling, and modulate the senescence-associated secretory phenotype by controlling inflammatory mediators, extracellular matrix remodeling, and angiogenic factors. Several of these miRNAs are also associated with resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy, taxanes, poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, and immunotherapies through effects on PI3K/AKT and Hippo signaling pathways, as well as DNA repair mechanisms. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to modulate or eliminate senescent cells using miRNA mimics, inhibitors, or gene-editing approaches, including nanoparticle-based delivery systems. Although preclinical studies suggest that these approaches may restore chemosensitivity, clinical translation remains limited by delivery challenges, off-target effects, and the context-dependent role of senescence. Targeting miRNA-senescence regulatory axes may represent a strategy for addressing drug resistance in ovarian cancer and warrants further investigation as part of combination treatment strategies.

abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is globally the leading cause of liver disease and frequently progresses to cirrhosis and liver cancer. The identification of effective drugs is the main unmet clinical need. Changes in liver histones methylation accompanies the development and progression of NAFLD. Our preliminary data demonstrate that inactivation of the methyltransferases SUV420H1/2 in hepatocytes protects mice against NAFLD. In this project we propose to examine the relevance of these findings by evaluating the impact of genetic deletion of hepatic SUV420H1/2 in mice fed a steatogenic diet. To further evaluate the potential for clinical translation of these results, we will next 1) evaluate the expression of SUV420H1/2 in human liver transcriptomic data and 2) analyze the impact of genetic variations on disease outcomes in population-based cohorts; 3) test an innovative therapeutic approach based on hepatocyte-targeted antisense oligonucleotides downregulating SUV420H1/2 in human liver organoids/assembloids.

description:
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), the leading cause of liver damage worldwide, is characterized by liver fat accumulation and association with insulin resistance, and frequently progresses to steatohepatitis (NASH), ultimately leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

NAFLD/NASH is becoming globally a leading cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality and by altering liver function contributes more widely to the burden of cardiometabolic, renal and neoplastic diseases. In the presence of concomitant hepatotoxic factors such as in particular atrisk alcohol intake and some medications (defined in this case as metabolic dysfunction associated fatty liver disease or MAFLD) synergizes with them representing a major driver of liver disease progression. However, for those with advanced disease or who cannot successfully change their diet and lifestyle, no effective treatment is yet available to prevent or treat this condition, which is therefore projected to become a major public health threat in the next decade. Although understanding the mechanisms of NAFLD development and progression is essential for its prevention/treatment, molecular players involved in its progression are poorly defined. Recently, an epigenetic component is recognized in this disorder and the histone methyltransferases SUV420H1/2 are promising candidates for this function. Multiple evidences connect lipid and iron metabolism in the hepatocyte: 1) Genome Wide Association Studies (GWAS) in human populations showed an overlap of loci affecting iron and lipid metabolism, and excess iron in hepatocytes favors dyslipidemia and NAFLD; 2) upregulation of the liver hormone hepcidin, under the control by the BMP-SMAD pathway, is protective against NAFLD-NASH. Interestingly, a GWAS performed in mouse strains kept on high-iron diet identified a shared association between liver iron and triglyceride levels at a region of chromosome 7 encompassing the histone methyltransferase Suv420h2. Our preliminary data show that mice with Suv420h inactivation in adipose tissue are resistant to diet-induced liver steatosis due to increased PPAR signaling. Since mice with liver BMP-SMAD pathway upregulation showed Suv420h downregulation, we hypothesize that the protective effect of increased hepatocyte BMP-SMAD signaling on NAFLD development is due to Suv420h. In agreement, Suv420h inactivation in hepatocytes counteracts diet-induced NAFLD, as highlighted by our preliminary results.

The present study is part of the RF project (Ricerca Finalizzata) - Project code: RF-2021-12373889 funded by the grant call of the Ministery of Health (2020-2021). In the attached project we proposed 3 different aims:

* To characterize the disease progression in Suv420h1/2-liver conditional KO mice and to identify
* To examine the impact of SUV420H1/2 genetic, epigenetic and transcriptional variability on clinical outcomes for the identification of novel biomarkers of NAFLD-NASH.
* To propose and test an innovative therapeutic approach based on hepatocyte-targeted antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) against Suv420h1/2 in preclinical models in mice and in human liver organoids and assembloids. The present clinical study protocol will focus on the clinical aspects and procedures that will regard an intervention on data and sample of clinical cohorts. Further details about the analyses conducted in animal models, for which a specific Authorization has been requested, can be found in the attached project.

outcomes.description:
The primary aim is the identification of biological pathways differentially ex- pressed in NAFLD individuals.

Considering the large number of individuals with severe liver disease in the NAFLD PERSPECTIVE and MAFALDA cohorts (n= 500) and the large size of UKBB population-based cohort (n=350,000 for common variants and n=200,000 for rare variants), for variants with a minor allele frequency (MAF) \>0.01, we estimated that the study has a power \>80% to detect six-fold difference in the risk of severe NAFLD in the PERSPECTIVE/MAFALDA, a 1.8% difference in the NAFLD prevalence (UK Biobank), and 4.4% difference in the liver fat content as measured by PDFF (UK Biobank) between carriers and non-carriers (Aim A and B).

abstract:
PURPOSE: MEDI1191 is a lipid nanoparticle-formulated messenger RNA (mRNA) designed to induce local interleukin (IL) 12 production and intensify antitumor T-cell responses. We report dose-escalation results from a first-in-human, open-label, phase I study of intratumoral MEDI1191 plus intravenous durvalumab (NCT03946800).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients were ≥18 years with advanced/metastatic solid tumors and had progressed on ≥1 line of prior therapy (immunotherapy permitted). Cutaneous/subcutaneous (parts 1A and 1B) or deep-seated lesions (part 1D) were injected; patients had ≥1 noninjected lesion measurable per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST v1.1). Target lesions were noninjected. MEDI1191 and durvalumab were given sequentially (part 1A) or concurrently (parts 1B and 1D). Primary objectives were safety and determination of maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary objectives included efficacy.
RESULTS: As of February 27, 2023, 61 patients were treated. Patients had a median of four prior regimens (range, 1-17); 39 (63.9%) received prior anti-programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death ligand 1 [PD-(L)1] immunotherapy. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) occurred in 96.7% of patients, and 41.0% experienced grade 3/4 TEAEs. There were no dose-limiting toxicities. The MTD was not reached. The objective response rate was 9.8%, including 1 confirmed complete response and 5 confirmed partial responses (PR). The duration of response was 2.7 to 22.3 months; the median was not reached. Responses occurred in injected lesions, local noninjected lesions, and distant lesions. Three of the 39 patients with prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy had PRs.
CONCLUSIONS: MEDI1191 and durvalumab were tolerated. Preliminary antitumor activity was encouraging in these heavily pretreated patients, including patients previously treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.

abstract: Glioma, particularly glioblastoma, remains difficult to treat because of limited drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, profound immune suppression, and insufficient intracranial exposure of systemic immunotherapies. Intranasal nano-immunotherapy is being explored as a potential strategy that may integrate noninvasive nose-to-brain delivery with nanocarrier-mediated immune reprogramming. Intranasal administration may partially bypass conventional vascular barriers through olfactory, trigeminal, mucosal, cerebrospinal-fluid, and perivascular transport routes, while nanoparticles are designed to protect immune-active payloads, support brain tumor targeting, and enable controlled release. Current evidence spans three distinct levels: direct intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy, intranasal glioma nanodelivery without demonstrated immune reprogramming, and non-intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy that provides mechanistic support for future intranasal adaptation. Across these evidence levels, investigated platforms include peptide-guided nanomicelles, lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic nanoparticles, ferritin-based nanovectors, spherical nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, bacterial outer membrane vesicles, and stimuli-responsive systems. These platforms can deliver immune-activating cargos, such as STING or TLR agonists; gene-regulatory cargos, such as siRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 components; and microenvironment-modulating cargos, such as chemokine-axis inhibitors, checkpoint-modulating agents, and combination payloads. Through these payloads, intranasal nanoplatforms may activate innate immune sensing, reverse myeloid-mediated suppression, enhance T-cell infiltration, and induce immunogenic cell death. However, translation remains limited by dosing uncertainty, species differences in nasal anatomy, mucosal and neurological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and incomplete immune pharmacodynamic validation. This review summarizes recent advances in intranasal and brain-targeted glioma nano-immunotherapy, highlights key immune mechanisms, and proposes a preclinical validation framework for evaluating whether experimental efficacy can be advanced toward clinically testable treatment designs.

abstract:
This study is researching an experimental drug called ALN-CIDEB, also referred to as "study drug". The study is focused on participants with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (Part A) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) (Part B). MASLD and MASH are long-lasting liver conditions caused by having too much fat in the liver.

The aim of the study is to see how safe and tolerable the study drug is.

The study is looking at several other research questions, including:

* What side effects may happen from taking the study drug
* How the study drug works to change liver fat content
* How much study drug and study drug metabolites (byproducts of the body breaking down the study drug) are in the blood at different times

abstract: Genetic engineering can transform bacteria (including Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Listeria, and Yersinia) from naturally occurring microbes into programmable therapeutics. Unlike passive platforms, engineered bacteria can localize to defined biological niches, sense environmental cues, regulate programmed activity in situ, interact with host tissues in novel ways, and persist for controlled periods. These properties make bacteria versatile medicines but require genetic control of precision, safety, stability, and activity under clinical conditions. Major design layers include strain or "chassis" selection, attenuation and biocontainment, control of therapeutic activity, targeting and persistence, and genotype-to-phenotype stability during manufacturing and in vivo use. These features also create liabilities, including off-target behavior, unstable expression, and evolutionary loss of function under selection. Progress depends on safe, clinically translatable chassis with integrated, bounded, and durable behaviors. This review examines the genetic design principles and liabilities of bacteria-based therapeutics, approaches used to produce clinical and near-clinical candidates, and the emergence of programmed bacteria delivering complete gene editing systems to therapeutically relevant cells.

abstract: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

title: Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses.

abstract: Myeloid cells regulate immune exclusion, T-cell dysfunction, angiogenesis, stromal remodeling, and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade in solid tumors. Pharmacological development has moved from nonspecific depletion toward recruitment or survival blockade, intracellular state reprogramming, restoration of antigen presentation, and tumor-selective phagocytosis. Clinical experience nevertheless shows a recurrent gap between biological activity and attributable therapeutic immune conversion. We introduce the Myeloid Immune Conversion Audit Trail (MICAT), a fixed four-level extension of the pharmacological audit trail that grades intratumoral target engagement, conversion of the intended myeloid state, propagation through the immune ecosystem, and randomized clinical attribution. Each level is scored as not demonstrated, partial, or demonstrated. Applying MICAT across representative trials shows that most programs stop at systemic pharmacodynamics or partial lineage effects; few establish ecosystem propagation, and none yet completes the entire causal chain for an immunological switch in a solid-tumor carcinoma. The analysis identifies compensation and redundancy as the central biological obstacle: CCR2 blockade can recruit CXCR2-positive neutrophils, CSF1R inhibition can spare resistant SPP1-high macrophages, and CD40 or PI3Kγ activation can induce interferon-linked PD-L1 feedback. We therefore prioritize lineage-resolved paired tissue, preservation of cDC1 and cDC2 function, absolute cell quantification, orthogonal functional and spatial readouts, and randomized component-controlled trials. Disease context is decisive: tenosynovial giant-cell tumor establishes CSF1R dependence without proving immune conversion; macrophage-rich triple-negative breast cancer is a rational PI3Kγ test-bed; pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma permits sequence-aware CD40 and stromal studies; and microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer is a stringent failure benchmark. CAR-macrophages, in vivo mRNA/lipid-nanoparticle reprogramming, myeloid engagers, and artificial-intelligence-assisted spatial scoring are mapped to the same evidence requirements. MICAT is intended as a reproducible tool for pharmacological go/no-go decisions rather than a claim that target modulation alone constitutes therapeutic immune conversion.

title: Corrigendum to "In vitro activation of anti-cancer gene expression by delivery of CRISPR/dCas9 ribonucleoproteins to suppress glioblastoma" [Int. J. Biol. Macromol. 308P1 (2025) 142289].

abstract:
PURPOSE: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is important in promoting a pro-oncogenic tumor microenvironment. This first randomized trial of a STAT3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide with pembrolizumab assessed whether this first-line combination would improve outcomes compared with pembrolizumab alone in recurrent/metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label, controlled study (NCT05814666) enrolled patients with previously untreated R/M HNSCC with positive PD-L1 expression [combined positive score (CPS) ≥1]. Patients were stratified by CPS (1-19; ≥20) and randomized 2:1 to danvatirsen 3 mg/kg intravenously weekly (with two loading doses in week 1) plus pembrolizumab 200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks or pembrolizumab alone. Patients received 21-day treatment cycles until progressive disease, unacceptable toxicity, or voluntary withdrawal. Primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR; partial + complete response per RECIST v1.1).
RESULTS: Sixty-nine patients were randomized, and 66 were treated [51 (77.3%) male]: 45 with danvatirsen + pembrolizumab and 21 with pembrolizumab alone. Enrollment was stopped due to lack of response in the CPS 1 to 19 cohort after ≥1 scan (∼6 weeks of treatment) and in the CPS ≥20 cohort after ≥2 scans (∼12 weeks). In the final analysis, ORRs were 15.6% and 14.3%, respectively (risk difference 1.3; P = 1). The treatment-emergent adverse event rate was increased in the combination arm (97.8% vs. 85.7%), and the combination side effect profile was similar to previous danvatirsen studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Combination danvatirsen + pembrolizumab did not improve ORR compared with pembrolizumab alone in first-line treatment of R/M HNSCC. Further exploration of STAT3-targeted approaches is needed within the context of immunotherapy.

title: Danvatirsen plus Pembrolizumab versus Pembrolizumab for Recurrent and/or Metastatic Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (PEMDA-HN): A Randomized, Phase II Trial.

abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics (NATs), including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics and programmable editing technologies, are reshaping the therapeutic landscape for inherited metabolic and genetic disease. Unlike conventional small molecules or biologics, NATs enable sequence-directed modulation of target gene expression and therefore provide unprecedented flexibility for targeting pathogenic mechanisms previously considered undruggable. Recent clinical successes have established proof of concept for multiple NAT modalities across neurological, hepatic, muscular and metabolic disorders. However, broader implementation remains constrained by challenges in tissue-specific delivery, biomarker validation, natural-history infrastructure and evidence generation in ultra-rare populations. In parallel, increasing platform reproducibility is beginning to challenge traditional product-based regulatory paradigms. This review examines the principal classes of NATs and proposes a practical framework for modality selection based on disease biology, tissue accessibility, durability, reversibility and clinical context. We discuss key translational bottlenecks beyond delivery, including biomarker-outcome relationships, small-population trial design and the limitations of conventional evidentiary frameworks in rare disease. A central theme of this review is the growing transition from isolated precision medicines towards increasingly programmable therapeutic platforms. We explore how advances in extrahepatic delivery, computational oligonucleotide design, artificial intelligence-assisted optimisation and programmable editing technologies may progressively support more scalable and individualised therapeutic development. Finally, we discuss emerging regulatory frameworks that may better accommodate platform-level predictability while maintaining rigorous evaluation of sequence-specific and disease-specific risks.

title: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Rare Disease: From Precision Medicine to Programmable Platforms.

abstract: Effective delivery of RNA therapeutics to the brain remains challenging due to the multiple barriers of the central nervous system (CNS). To probe molecular scaffolds that could help overcome these barriers, we analysed the pharmaceutical profiles of over 100 CNS-active drugs and identified hydroxyzine (HX) as a promising scaffold for designing ionizable lipids with improved brain-targeting properties. Specifically, HX1 liquid nanoparticles (LNPs) achieved robust mRNA delivery to the brain through multiple trafficking pathways across CNS barriers. HX1 LNPs also enabled efficient gene editing in mouse brains via co-delivery of CRISPR mRNA and guide RNA and effectively delivered luciferase mRNA to the brain of a non-human primate. Moreover, HX1 LNPs carrying Il10 mRNA mitigated radiation-induced brain injury in mice, highlighting their potential for preventive treatment in the presence of intact CNS barriers. These findings establish HX1 LNPs as a promising translational platform for delivering therapeutic mRNAs and genome-editing components to the brain.

title: Rational design of lipid nanoparticles for brain delivery of RNA therapeutics.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is prone to relapse driven by therapy-persistent residual cells. To discover specific vulnerabilities in this population, we performed genome-wide CRISPR interference screens in leukemia cells treated with multiple agents. KHSRP was the top hit, the depletion of which sensitized AML cells to therapy and substantially prolonged survival in treated AML-bearing mice. Analysis of in vivo residual disease after venetoclax/azacitidine treatment identified downregulation of the vitamin C and uric acid transporter SLC23A1, which mediated resistance to multiple therapies. KHSRP depletion restored SLC23A1 expression by preventing its ZC3H4-mediated nuclear mRNA degradation. KHSRP depletion therefore enhanced the synergistic cytotoxicity of vitamin C and uric acid, particularly in therapy-persistent leukemia cells. Re-expression of TET2 overrode the chemosensitizing effect of KHSRP depletion in TET2-mutant leukemia, suggesting that KHSRP-linked phenotypes were related to vitamin C- and uric acid-mediated TET activation. These findings suggest targeting KHSRP to enhance treatment efficacy and selectively eradicate residual AML.
SIGNIFICANCE: Residual AML cells that persist following therapy have distinct biological properties compared with initial disease or overt relapse. Here, we nominate KHSRP as a target to improve therapy efficacy and exploit selective vulnerabilities of AML residual disease.

abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics (ONTs) have revolutionized the medical landscape by enabling the precise modulation of genetic pathways. This perspective highlights the major conjugation strategies for ONTs, using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) as representative modalities. We describe diverse classes of targeting ligands, including small molecules, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), antibodies, and aptamers. For example, triantennary N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) conjugation has enabled a number of approved oligonucleotide therapeutics. Meanwhile, other emerging conjugation technologies have expanded oligonucleotide delivery to extrahepatic tissues to address a broader range of diseases. We further summarize the clinical translation of these delivery platforms, highlighting approved therapeutics alongside emerging clinical candidates. Finally, we provide an outlook on challenges and opportunities for the next generation of oligonucleotide therapeutics.

title: Advances in therapeutic oligonucleotide conjugates.

abstract: Stargardt disease is caused by biallelic variants in the ABCA4 gene and is the most frequent autosomal recessive macular degeneration in childhood and adolescence. No approved disease-modifying treatment has yet been approved. The size of the ABCA4 gene represents a challenge for conventional gene therapy based on adeno-associated viruses (AAV) and was the stimulus for the development of innovative strategies. Gene supplementation therapies use lentiviral or dual AAV vectors to introduce complete copies of the healthy ABCA4 gene into the target cells, whereas gene editing procedures, such as RNA exon editing or base editing, enable direct correction of the mutations causing the diseases. Intravitreal injection of antisense oligonucleotides selectively addresses splicing defects and provides a less invasive intravitreal approach but requires repeated applications. Indirect therapies modulate the visual cycle or neuroprotective signalling pathways and can be applied independent of variants. Finally, disease-agnostic approaches, such as optogenetics, enable restoration of vision in cases of advanced degeneration by the use of preserved inner retinal layers. The diversity of these approaches takes account of the broad spectrum of diseases that ranges from a disease limited to the macula to a generalized rod-cone dystrophy and perspectively opens up individualized treatment strategies depending on the genotype and phenotype.

title: [Genetic therapies for Stargardt disease].

abstract: We have previously proposed a combined therapy for spinal muscular atrophy based on the upregulation of exon 7 (E7) inclusion into SMN2 mRNA by the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen (ASO1) together with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using a CRISPR-deadCas-based strategy in a human cell line, we show here that targeting histone acetylation at the SMN2 E7 region duplicates the HDACi effect, which overcomes pleiotropic effects. Most noticeably, targeted acetylation at the E7 region causes acetylation and activation of the 30-kbp-distant promoter. Since the nusinersen target site maps near the SMN2 gene 3' end, this crosstalk between the two ends of the gene prompted us to use chromosome conformation analysis (3C) to find that ASO1 promotes gene looping. This unpredicted property of ASOs in modulating chromatin 3D configuration depends on cohesin, CTCF, cleavage/polyadenylation factors, and a canonical poly(A) signal and causes promoter activation at a long distance, which expands the therapeutic potential of splicing-correcting ASOs.

title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing targeting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer has transformed therapeutic approaches for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (β-thal) and sickle cell disease (SCD). Even though clinical efficacy is well demonstrated, translating these therapies to global patient populations requires a strong evidence-based framework to address critical concerns regarding long-term genotoxic safety and long-lasting engraftment dynamics.
METHODS: Following the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review of 21 key clinical and preclinical studies (published during 2014-2026) to evaluate CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in β-thal and SCD. The inclusion criteria focused on studies reporting foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction, transfusion independence (TI) and safety outcomes.
RESULTS: Clinical data indicate high efficacy, with exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) achieving TI in 91% of β-thal patients and a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)-free status in 97% of SCD patients. Safety profiling confirmed that severe adverse events, including febrile neutropenia and stomatitis, are primarily associated with busulfan-based myeloablation rather than gene editing. Gene-editing safety and conditioning toxicity are interlinked because conditioning is part of the process, and edited clones might interact with stress pathways during long-term repopulation. Preclinical benchmarks substantiate molecular reliability, with negligible off-target activity reported in most validated platforms. However, rare instances of complex structural rearrangements and intergenic off-target indels highlight the necessity for in-depth, unbiased long-term genomic surveillance.
CONCLUSION: CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-thal and SCD treatment constitute a treatment option within current clinical frameworks. These therapies need continuous surveillance. Rather than establishing a perfect plan, this systematic review highlights that while current platforms are thought to have short-term molecular precision, the use of Multilayer Safety Risks Screening and Surveillance for pretransplant conditioning is critical. This approach helps address long-term genotoxic concerns and ensures the safety and scalability of gene-editing therapies for global β-thal and SCD patient care.

title: Genotoxic safety and long-term engraftment dynamics of efficient translational CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-haemoglobinopathies from bench to clinical trials.

abstract: Endogenous retrotransposable elements (ERE) can modulate immune responses. We explored ERE transcription in relation to response to immune checkpoint inhibition in advanced solid tumors. ERE expression was measured in pre- and on-treatment samples from patients treated in a clinical trial with pembrolizumab. We evaluated immune cell infiltration and correlated ERE expression with interferon (IFN)-stimulated gene profiles and cytolytic activity. Two independent datasets were retrospectively analyzed as external validation. ERE transcription, notably Alu repetitive elements followed by long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE), is upregulated in immunotherapy responders, and higher ERE expression correlates with durable clinical benefit and improved long-term outcomes. In responders, this dynamic increase correlates with CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytolytic activity, particularly during treatment. A trend toward increased A-to-I RNA editing was observed in responders. External validation in melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts confirmed a consistent pattern in ERE transcription. Therefore, ERE transcription is emerging as a potential biomarker for personalized immunotherapy in solid tumors.

title: Immune Checkpoint Blockade Sensitivity Is Linked to Endogenous Retroelement Transcriptional Changes in Cancer.

abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) progression involves cartilage matrix loss and persistent inflammation. This study developed a machine learning-guided and chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticle carrying messenger RNA (CM-LNP@mRNA) platform for intra-articular SOX9 delivery. Random forest analysis identified the nitrogen-to-phosphorus and SM-102 ratios as primary determinants with feature importance values of 0.57 and 0.32 respectively. Following ML-guided formulation selection and experimental membrane-coating optimization, the final CM-LNP@mRNA formulation showed an encapsulation efficiency of 95.50% and a particle size of 133.70 nm. Compared with the conventional reference formulation prepared under the same final coating condition, encapsulation efficiency increased from 89.20% to 95.50% and particle size decreased from 145.40 nm to 133.70 nm. Membrane coating shifted the zeta potential from -25.57 mV to -35.07 mV. This transition provided biophysical evidence of successful surface modification. In interleukin-1β-stimulated chondrocytes, CM-LNP@mRNA increased the relative expression of Col2a1 and Acan from 0.20 to 0.33 and from 0.50 to 0.73, respectively, while reducing the relative expression of Mmp3 and Adamts5 from 10.50 to 7.80 and from 4.00 to 2.50, respectively. These alterations indicated a shift toward a matrix-preserving transcriptional state. Downstream matrix metalloproteinase 3 and prostaglandin E2 concentrations decreased from 37.10 ng/mL to 18.50 ng/mL and from 113.70 pg/mL to 76.50 pg/mL by day 7. This reduction demonstrated effective suppression of catabolic and inflammatory activity. In OA rats, CM-LNP@mRNA reduced the osteophyte volume from 4.00 mm3 to 2.00 mm3 and prolonged the thermal response latency from 7.50 s to 11.80 s. These improvements linked cellular metabolic regulation to functional joint recovery. These findings establish a strategy integrating formulation optimization with biomimetic membrane coating to modulate the OA microenvironment.

title: Machine learning-guided chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticles for intra-articular SOX9 mRNA therapy of osteoarthritis.

abstract: Frailty, an age-related state of increased vulnerability, is associated with greater susceptibility to infection and impaired vaccine response. In this Review, we examine how frailty-associated immunosenescence, including altered haematopoiesis, chronic inflammation, and dysfunction of innate and adaptive immune responses, can affect the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines. Evidence from COVID-19 lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines and other vaccines suggests that people living with frailty can mount weaker or less durable responses than non-frail peers, although findings remain heterogeneous and frailty-specific evidence is scarce. The high customisability of lipid nanoparticle mRNA platforms creates opportunities for frailty-tailored vaccination. We discuss optimisation of lipid nanoparticle composition, targeting and dosing, mRNA cargo and combination-vaccine approaches, alongside host-directed measures addressing comorbidities, nutrition, and immune dysfunction. Integrating frailty into vaccine design, evaluation, and deployment could support safer, more effective, and more individualised vaccination strategies for older adults.

abstract: Targeted modulation of microglial activation with siRNA in neuroinflammatory diseases presents a compelling therapeutic strategy by enabling precise gene silencing while preserving beneficial immune responses. However, the immune-sensitive nature of microglia creates unique barriers to safe and efficient siRNA delivery. Dual pH- and redox-responsive polycationic nanogels with tunable molecular architectures are developed to overcome these barriers, enabling spatiotemporal delivery and intracellular degradation. Varying hydrophilic and hydrophobic monomer ratios tunes nanogel molecular architecture to control particle size, pH-responsive behavior, and therapeutic release. Disulfide crosslinkers enable selective degradation of polymer networks into fragments at intracellular glutathione levels, enabling controlled release and intracellular degradation. Increased hydrophobic composition yields smaller hydrodynamic size, optimal pH swelling profile for endosomal escape, and surface charge shifts that balance membrane disruption and biocompatibility. Degradation studies confirm redox-responsive crosslinks selective fragmentation at intracellular glutathione levels. Systematic siRNA loading studies demonstrate electrostatic interactions dominate, achieving high loading efficiency. Release studies mimicking intracellular environmental shifts confirm the spatiotemporal siRNA delivery from dual-responsive nanogels. Nanogels demonstrate first-pass cytocompatibility (MTS and LDH assays) with microglia at therapeutic concentrations. Both formulations achieve intracellular accumulation of carboxyfluorescein (FAM)-labelled siRNA in microglia, with higher efficacy for the more hydrophobic formulation. Future work will investigate the platform's innate immune response in microglia and functional knockdown of disease-relevant genes with target specific siRNA to modulate microglia's neuroinflammatory response. Collectively, these dual-responsive nanogels provide a foundational rational design framework for vectors that balance biosafety and delivery efficacy for siRNA therapies to microglia for targeting neuroinflammation.

title: Rational design of polycationic, biodegradable nanogels for intracellular siRNA delivery to microglia.

abstract: The ability of an organism to identify self and foreign RNA is central to eliciting an immune response in times of need while avoiding autoimmunity. As viral pathogens typically employ double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), host identification, modulation, and response to dsRNA is key. However, dsRNA is also abundant in host transcriptomes, raising the question of how these molecules can be differentiated. Two host pathways that regulate dsRNA are A-to-I RNA editing by adenosine deaminases (ADARs), and RNA interference (RNAi). Both mechanisms are important for normal organism development and function by regulating gene expression. Herein, we studied the structure and amount of siRNAs at editing sites and the ability of ADARs to prevent exogenous RNAi using the model organism, Caenorhabditis elegans. We found that the number of siRNAs targeting edited genes is significantly upregulated in ADAR mutant animals. We also found that despite an almost complete depletion of primary siRNAs generated from editing sites in wildtype animals, secondary siRNAs are generated from edited transcripts, suggesting ADARs antagonize only the first step of RNAi processing. We show that ADARs interfere with the efficacy of exogenous RNAi in vivo, probably to prevent trans-silencing, and have indications that ADR-2 binding to the dsRNA is needed for the efficient prevention of RNAi. This work sheds light on how the RNA editing process protects self-produced dsRNAs from aberrant recognition by the immune processes in the cell and from by-product degradation.

abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, most of which are large exon deletions that result in loss of dystrophin protein. Adenine base editing (ABE) enables permanent gene correction by modifying splice sites to cause exon skipping and restoration of the DMD open reading frame. We previously demonstrated that adeno-associated virus 9-mediated (AAV9-mediated) delivery of adenine base editors allows efficient gene editing in mouse models of DMD. However, conventional AAV-based gene delivery approaches are complicated by their limited packaging capacity and high-dose-related toxicity. Here, we describe a single AAV vector encoding a compact adenine base editor, SlugABE8e, and a single-guide RNA, which enable efficient editing in a humanized DMD mouse model at a lower dose using the muscle-tropic MyoAAV4 capsid. Systemic MyoAAV4A delivery in juvenile DMD mice efficiently restored dystrophin expression in the heart and skeletal muscles. This molecular rescue was accompanied by reduced serum creatine kinase activity and diminished muscle pathology. A liver-detargeted MyoAAV4E-off capsid eliminated viral entry and editing in the liver. We also explored a high-fidelity base editor, SlugHF-ABE8e(V106W), which showed similar on-target and off-target editing to SlugABE8e. Together, these findings establish an all-in-one AAV strategy that efficiently mitigates DMD disease progression.

abstract: BackgroundJNJ-73763989 is a 2:1 combination of 2 N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated short interfering RNAs (siRNA) targeting the S (daplusiran) and X (tomligisiran) regions of the hepatitis B virus genome. In phase 2b studies, 48 weeks of JNJ-73763989-based combination treatments led to dose-dependent reductions in viral markers, including hepatitis B surface antigen. The objective of the INSIGHT study Panel 3 was to quantify intrahepatic concentrations of the siRNAs in human livers during and after treatment.MethodsIn the open-label, single-arm, single-center study, participants with chronic hepatitis B received 48 weeks of treatment with JNJ-73763989 200 mg every 4 weeks and nucleos(t)ide analog, with optional pegylated interferon α2a 180 µg weekly added after Treatment Week (TW) 40. Core liver biopsies were collected at TW12, TW40, and at Follow-up Week (FUW) 24.ResultsLiver biopsies were available from all 4 participants at TW12 and from 3 at TW40 and FUW24. Between TW12 and TW40, liver concentrations of daplusiran and tomligisiran increased 1.5- to 2.6-fold, consistent with intrahepatic accumulation. Twenty-eight weeks after the last injection of JNJ-73763989, the triggers were still measurable in 2 of 3 participants with 4.5- to 15-fold reduced concentrations from peak levels; the estimated liver half-life ranged from approximately 2.9 to 16.1 weeks.ConclusionsIn this first study to assess liver concentrations of GalNAc-siRNA in humans with sequential biopsies, long persistence of JNJ-73763989 triggers in human livers may partially explain the prolonged suppressive effect on viral parameters observed in phase 2 studies.

abstract: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) convert adenosine positioned within double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to inosine (A-to-I). This reaction can be redirected to a specific target transcript by exogenous guide RNAs (gRNAs) that recruit abundant endogenous ADARs without the need for exogenous protein delivery. Approximately 16,000 pathogenic G > A mutations are correctable by A-to-I conversion, thus representing a broad scope for therapeutic A-to-I editing. This review covers the key advances in gRNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing. We first discuss how ADAR biology informs rational gRNA design. We then survey gRNA design strategies that increase on-target editing efficiency and diminish bystander editing. Delivery modalities are then discussed for both unmodified and modified gRNAs as a strategy to minimize transcriptome-wide off-target editing. We conclude by outlining the outstanding challenges and future opportunities, including computational gRNA design, to guide the next generation of gRNAs towards the path of approved RNA editing medicines.

title: Advances in guide RNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated therapeutic RNA editing.

abstract: Gene therapy has transformed modern biomedical research by enabling curative strategies that target the molecular basis of disease. Among genome-editing technologies, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a versatile and efficient platform due to its programmability, simplicity, and precision. This review summarizes the evolution of gene therapy and highlights the therapeutic potential of CRISPR-based genome editing. CRISPR/Cas9 has demonstrated significant potential in correcting disease-causing mutations across multiple inherited disorders, including sickle cell disease, β- thalassemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, phenylketonuria, muscular dystrophies, and cystic fibrosis. Emerging technologies such as base editing and prime editing further improved editing precision and reduced unintended genomic alterations. However, challenges including off-target effects, DNA repair pathway bias, immune responses, and vector-associated toxicities remain major limitations. The review highlights the rapid progress of CRISPR-mediated therapeutics and emphasizes the importance of improving editing accuracy, delivery efficiency, and long-term safety. Advances in vector engineering and genome-editing platforms are expected to overcome current technical and ethical barriers, facilitating broader clinical applications. CRISPR/Cas9 and related genome- editing technologies represent promising disease-modifying and potentially curative therapeutic approaches. Continued optimization of precision, safety, and delivery systems will be essential for successful translation into routine clinical practice.

abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of bio-chemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg 2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between G exo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5 ' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the G exo in the first step, and analogously the G ω in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the p K a at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.

abstract: Genome-targeting strategies to address NaV1.7-mediated signaling in nociceptive afferents are of great clinical interest given its high selectivity and persistent analgesic outcomes. In the present work, we analyze concentration-dependent effects of suppressing primary afferent NaV1.7 using the intrathecal delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) on pain behaviors and demonstrate that NaV1.7 ASOs are likely to modulate pain traffic by blocking afferent signaling at the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) level. Intrathecal NaV1.7 ASOs induced a concentration-dependent gradient of knockdown in DRGs (lumbar to cervical) of Scn9a mRNA and ATTO488-ProTx-II binding in small DRG neurons, and a suppression of pain behaviors initiated by mechanical compression, inflammation, and the NaV1.7 agonist OD-1. The rostro-caudal reduction in mRNA correlated with ASO distribution, with implications for dose-related analgesic profiles. Marked reduction in DRG NaV1.7 binding was seen after intrathecal delivery of an ASO optimal dose, with high selectivity for small DRG neurons. Changes in sciatic nerve NaV1.7 binding were not detected, indicating a pain traffic modulation likely happening due to a block of afferent signaling at the DRG level.

abstract: Delivering therapeutic mRNA relies on lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Finding optimal process parameters for new lipid combinations in LNP formulations remains a challenge. We used an automated, self-regulating microfluidic formulation platform developed for PEG-containing LNPs that actively changes process parameters to meet preset LNP diameters, and now explore how this automated production setup can be expanded to LNPs decorated with poly(2-oxazoline) (POx)-lipids. We also examine how the choice of lipopolymer affects the resulting physicochemical properties and in vivo biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. For that, we tested new LNPs by swapping poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipopolymers for alternatives based on poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) (PMeOx) and poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx). For both POx-lipid variants, the platform independently identified optimal production conditions in four or fewer iterative cycles, yielding particles of the preset size and high mRNA encapsulation. Small-angle X-ray scattering revealed that smaller LNPs modified with PEtOx had greater structural surface variety and higher mRNA loading efficiency. When multiplexing these formulations in mice, the PEtOx-containing LNPs accumulated more in bone marrow and liver (and less in spleen and pancreas), compared to those with PEG, indicating trends that the chemistry of the lipopolymer affects the biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. By combining automated formulation and in vivo multiplexed testing, our approach provides a practical way to rapidly plan, formulate, and evaluate large pharmaceutical design spaces to select excipients and process parameters yielding optimal biological performance of LNPs.

title: Exploring lipid nanoparticle design spaces using self-regulating microfluidic machines and multiplexed in vivo biodistribution.

abstract: Following the successes of the messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against COVID-19, mRNA-LNPs are being explored for varied multidose applications including cancer immunotherapies and protein replacement therapies. LNPs rely on poly(ethylene glycol)-lipid (PEG-lipid) coatings for stability, but increasing anti-PEG antibody prevalence threatens repeat-dose efficacy and increases pseudoallergic risk, creating an urgent need for alternatives. Here, we introduce poly(acrylamido) lipids (PAM-lipids), a family of polymer lipids that effectively replace PEG-lipids in mRNA-LNP formulations. Systematic variation of monomer chemistry, molar mass, and end group reveals critical structure-activity relationships determining LNP size, polydispersity, and transfection efficiency. Varying PAM monomer chemistry allows minimization of antipolymer antibody cross-reactivity, with multiple PAM-lipids demonstrating no anti-PEG antibody binding. Several PAM-LNPs exhibit superior mRNA transfection efficacy to PEGylated clinical benchmarks in vitro and in vivo across multiple cell types, organs, routes of administration, and mRNA cargos. In particular, lead PAM-LNPs enhance mRNA delivery to dendritic cells (up to 120-fold in vitro and 3-fold in vivo) and macrophages (4-fold in vivo), with 2.5-fold superior lymph node expression, driven in part by increased cellular association and lymphoid targeting. Crucially, PAM-LNPs evade circulating anti-PEG antibodies to rescue lost mRNA efficacy after repeated dosing, resulting in 300% mRNA expression relative to that of PEG-LNPs. These findings demonstrate PAM-lipids as a chemically varied, immunologically compatible family of PEG alternatives for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.

title: Poly(acrylamido) PEG-Alternative Lipids Rescue mRNA Efficacy during Repeated Dosing and Enhance Immune Cell Delivery.

abstract:
Background:

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a rare immune disorder caused by a mutation in the CYBB gene. People with CGD have white blood cells that do not work properly and are at greater risk of getting infections. Researchers want to know if gene therapy using the patient's own base-edited stem cells can improve the white cells' functioning and result in fewer CGD-related infections.

Objective:

To learn if base-edited stem cells will correct the white blood cells in people with CGD.

Eligibility:

Males aged 18 years and older with X-linked CGD.

Design:

This is a non-randomized study. Participants with the specific mutation under study will be screened during the initial phase.

During the development phase, participants will undergo apheresis to collect stem cells for base-editing correction of the mutation.

During the treatment phase, participants will first receive Campath (alemtuzumab) to reduce the risk of an immune response to the new protein expressed by the base-edited cells. This will be followed by conditioning chemotherapy with busulfan and subsequent infusion of the base-edited stem cells. Participants will be maintained on sirolimus to further reduce the risk of an immune response to the new protein expressed by the base-edited cells.

Follow-up visits will continue for 15 years....

description:
Study Description:

Open-label, phase 1/2 trial to determine the safety, and efficacy of a single infusion of base-edited (BE) autologous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) for treatment of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (X-CGD). Base editing is performed to repair CYBB missense gene mutations (eg, CYBB c.676C\>T). The study hypotheses are that 1) base editing can efficiently repair gene mutations in HSPCs; and 2) BE HSPCs can engraft and differentiate into functional phagocytes with restored nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase activity.

During the initial development phase each study participant will undergo apheresis for CD34+ HSPC collection for the development and validation of a mutation-specific BE system.

During the treatment phase, participants will receive a one-time infusion of the BE autologous HSPC (study product) after the administration of Campath (alemtuzumab) and of busulfan conditioning (total 12 mg/kg with a targeted total AUC of 65,000 ng/mL x hr). Sirolimus will be initiated on Day -1 and may be given for approximately 3-6 months.

Participants will have follow-up evaluations at months 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24, and yearly thereafter until 5 years after treatment. Key study assessments include adverse event (AE) assessment, blood laboratory evaluations of functional protein made from the target gene (CYBB, encodes for gp91\^phox), and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequencing to identify rates of gene repair and off-target mutation.

The final study follow-up under this protocol will be at 5 years, but long-term follow-up under a separate NIH protocol will continue annually to 15 years after treatment.

Objectives:

Primary Objectives:

* To evaluate the safety of BE autologous CD34+ cells.
* To evaluate the efficacy of BE autologous CD34+ cells.

Secondary Objectives:

-To evaluate:

* Efficiency of base editing (percentages of target nucleotide conversion).
* Engraftment capability of BE HSPCs.
* Efficiency in restoring gp91\^phox expression
* Efficiency in restoring NADPH oxidase function.
* Clinical efficacy.
* Stability of gene correction.

Exploratory Objectives:

-To evaluate:

* Specificity of base editing by assessing rates of off-target edits at top predicted sites.
* Random off-target edits by whole genome sequencing (WGS).

Endpoints:

Primary Endpoints:

* Safety of gene therapy using BE autologous HSPCs as measured by study product-related AEs and serious AEs (SAEs) through 2 years after treatment.
* Efficacy of gene therapy determined as percentages of subjects who have \>= 10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months after infusion.

Secondary Endpoints:

* Determine frequency of converted target nucleotide alleles.
* Assess the frequency of gene-modified alleles compared to infusion product in peripheral blood at 12 months.
* Evaluate efficacy of restoring gp91\^phox expression.
* Evaluate efficacy of NADPH oxidase functional restoration as measured by the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry oxidase assay at 12 months after treatment (\>=10% oxidase-positive neutrophils), or by quantitative measurement of reactive oxygen species (ROS) using the ferricytochrome C assay on peripheral blood granulocytes.
* Evaluate clinical benefit by improvement of baseline clinical problems such as recurrent infections, growth failure, malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, or antibiotic usage.
* Assess stability of gene correction by serial measurement of percent of nucleotide-converted alleles.

Exploratory Endpoints:

* Evaluate specificity by assessing for off-target edits at predicted sites with high-throughput sequencing of the 5 most common candidate off-target loci identified by a comprehensive in vitro screen, Circularization for High-throughput Analysis of Nuclease Genome-wide Effects by sequencing (CHANGE-seq-BE), in peripheral blood cells.
* Determine rate of random off-target edits WGS.

abstract: The main goal of the study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of GTX-102 in participants with Angelman syndrome.
description: This basket study is designed to evaluate safety and efficacy of GTX-102 in participants with Angelman syndrome across genotypes and age groups. The study consists of subprotocols A, B, C and D. All subprotocols are open-label and follow the same design which includes a Screening, Loading and Maintenance period. Subprotocols A, B and C are single arm only. In subprotocol D, participants are randomized 2:1 to a GTX-102 group or a No Treatment group. The No Treatment group follows the same schedule of events as all other groups after completion of the No Treatment period. Participants from all the subprotocols have the option to continue treatment in a long-term extension study following their end of study visit.

abstract:
The goal of this pilot clinical trial is to learn if tirzepatide can treat active central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a type of permanent scarring hair loss, in adults. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does tirzepatide improve the symptoms and signs of active CCCA?
* Does tirzepatide change the activity of genes in the scalp, especially genes related to scarring?
* Does tirzepatide promote hair regrowth?

Participants will:

* Inject tirzepatide once a week for 12 months.
* Visit the clinic for scalp examinations, photographs, and other health assessments.
* Have scalp biopsies at the beginning of the study and after 6 months of treatment.
* Have blood tests and other safety monitoring during the study.

There is no separate comparison group. Researchers will compare each participant's results during treatment with the participant's results at the beginning of the study.

abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to test the use of milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) in children with severe acute malnutrition in Sierra Leone. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Will the inclusion of MFGM in RUTF for 6-59-month-old Sierra Leonean children with severe acute malnutrition improve their neurodevelopment?
* Will the inclusion of MFGM in RUTF for 6-59-month-old Sierra Leonean children with severe acute malnutrition reduce its worst consequences: death, hospitalization, and remaining severely malnourished despite treatment?

Researchers will compare the MFGM-containing RUTF to standard RUTF, which contains skim milk powder.

Participants will:

* undergo measurement of length, weight, mid-upper arm circumference, and nutritional edema assessment every two weeks during severe malnutrition treatment
* be treated with either MFGM-RUTF or standard RUTF at a dose of 2 sachets per day for up to 12 weeks
* undergo neurodevelopmental testing using the Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool at the end of SAM treatment and 6 months later
* a subset of participants will undergo blood spot collection and stool sample collection

description:
Globally, approximately 15 million children are suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) at any one time, a number that has not declined in recent decades despite significant technological advancements in agriculture and food science. SAM is a condition of total-body depletion of the nutrients required for health and development; without treatment, 50% of affected children will die. Whereas historically children with SAM were admitted to and treated within hospitals, the advent of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) and community-based management of acute malnutrition revolutionized SAM care by allowing it to occur safely and successfully by the child's caregiver in their own home.

RUTF was designed to provide the nutrients required for physical recovery in a safe, palatable format. It is equal parts peanut paste, sugar, vegetable oil, and skim milk powder, with added micronutrients and emulsifier. At inception, attention was not specifically paid to how RUTF's composition might impact neurodevelopmental recovery in children with SAM. Research over the past decade has revealed that even following successful treatment with RUTF, children diagnosed with SAM still score 1-3 standard deviations below age-based expectations on neurodevelopmental tests. This suggests that the nutrient profile of standard RUTF is not sufficient to recover the developmental damage incurred by SAM.

Recently, progress has been made toward improving the developmental trajectory of children with SAM by altering RUTF. A randomized, blinded trial in Malawi including 2,500 children with SAM showed that improving the polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) profile of RUTF by reducing linoleic acid and adding docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) yields superior neurodevelopment 6 months after treatment, by 0.19 standard deviations on a standardized, culturally adapted neurodevelopmental test. This demonstrates that neurodevelopmental recovery in SAM is sensitive to the lipid profile of RUTF. Despite the benefits of improved PUFA RUTF, however, children with SAM remained 1 standard deviation below expectations in neurodevelopment.

The milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in mammalian milk contains a host of nutrients and bioactive compounds supportive of physical health and brain development. Bovine MFGM added to infant formula has been tested in several clinical trials and has demonstrated a reduction in infectious episodes, such as diarrhea and ear infections, as well as improvement in cognitive development, compared with infant formula not containing MFGM. In these trials and others, MFGM has been shown to be safe and well-tolerated. Currently, RUTF contains skim milk powder as its high-quality protein source, and peanut and vegetable oils as the primary sources of fat. These vegetable fat sources are deficient in the lipids provided by MFGM: sphingolipids, cholesterol, and other phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, all of which play roles in brain development. It is possible that the lipids contained in MFGM may further support neurodevelopmental recovery in SAM children.

By acting as a natural emulsifier, MFGM also offers a food formulation advantage that is relevant to children with SAM. Animal model studies have demonstrated that emulsifiers can compromise the gut barrier. Children with SAM have damaged small intestinal barrier function, which can lead to translocation of gut bacteria and resulting systemic infection. As RUTF will compose nearly 100% of a child's intake for the duration of treatment - up to 3 months - it is possible that inclusion of emulsifier may impede gut healing and recovery. Considering this concern, the Manary lab ran a clinical trial in 2018-2019 testing a novel formulation of RUTF designed with oat in place of some skim milk powder and peanut, and without hydrogenated vegetable oil (standard emulsifier), because oat acts as a natural emulsifier. In this trial, children with SAM receiving the oat-RUTF had 10% absolute higher recovery and a 33% relative reduction in the worst SAM outcomes (death, hospitalization, or remaining severely malnourished). Like oat, MFGM in RUTF allows for omission of emulsifier and may yield similar benefits.

Given (1) the repeated finding that adding MFGM to infant formulas improves neurodevelopment, (2) the impaired neurodevelopment of children with SAM, (3) the current RUTF formulation lacking neuro-supportive fats provided by MFGM, (4) MFGM's natural activity as an emulsifier, and (5), the reality that RUTF provides the sole source of nutrition for children with SAM, it is plausible that adding this high-quality source of lipids and protein to RUTF may also benefit children with SAM in both immediate and long-term physical and cognitive recovery.

This will be an individually randomized, investigator/outcomes assessors-blinded, controlled clinical trial designed to determine if treatment of severely malnourished Sierra Leonean children 6-59-months of age with an RUTF made with MFGM-containing whey protein/fat concentrate will (1) improve neurodevelopment and (2) reduce a composite of poor SAM outcomes (death, hospitalization, remaining severely malnourished), compared with standard RUTF (S-RUTF). This trial will be conducted at 20 rural sites in Sierra Leone. 1600 children will be randomized 1:1 to receive 2 sachets per day of either MFGM-RUTF or S-RUTF. Children will receive their allocated RUTF and return to clinic fortnightly for repeat anthropometric measurements, illness questions, and to receive more RUTF until they achieve a clinical outcome or for a maximum of 12 weeks, at which point they will undergo Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool (MDAT) testing. Participants will be asked to return to clinic 6 (5-7) months later for MDAT testing, the global z-score from which will be the trial's co-primary outcome. A subset of participants will undergo blood spot and/or stool sample collection at the end of SAM treatment.

abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intensive vascular proliferation that is essential for tumor growth. Recent studies indicate the existence of tumor-derived endothelial-like cells can arise from the differentiation of GBM stem cells (GSCs). The transcription factor brachyury plays a critical role in promoting stem cell identity and vasculogenesis during normal embryonic development. However, its involvement in endothelial-like differentiation of GSCs remains unknown. By integrating clinical bioinformatics from GBM databases with preclinical in vitro and in vivo models, including patient-derived GSC cell lines and xenografts, we found that brachyury is highly expressed in GBM tissues and correlates with angiogenesis genes. Our study demonstrated that brachyury is activated by fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), which subsequently promotes GSC differentiation into endothelial-like cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling. GSCs with high brachyury expression display great sensitivity to selective FGFR inhibitors in vascular tube formation assays. In vivo pharmacological targeting of FGFR1 with inhibitor E7090 or brachyury gene editing using Cas9/gRNA suppresses GBM neovascularization and tumor growth. Furthermore, gene signature analysis of GBM patients further demonstrated that a lower FGFR1/brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signature score significantly correlates with favorable overall survival outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of FGFR1-driven brachyury activation in GSC-derived neovascularization and suggest that targeting the FGFR1-directed brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling represents a promising therapeutic strategy for GBM.

title: FGFR1-driven brachyury promotes endothelial-like differentiation of glioblastoma stem cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling pathways.

abstract: Engineering autologous T cells for adoptive therapies has revolutionized cancer treatment, yet limited persistence remains a major barrier to robust clinical responses and durable disease control. Although costimulation with 4-1BB markedly improves CAR-T-cell persistence, no comparably effective approach has been identified to enhance persistence in T-cell therapies that rely on native TCR signaling, including conventional TCR-T cells and synthetic T-cell receptor and antigen receptor (STAR) T cells. To identify intrinsic persistence regulators in a TCR-based context, we performed an in vivo CRISPR activation screen in STAR-T cells and identified the noncanonical NF-κB axis, with RELB as the top hit. Direct RELB overexpression, however, exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, motivating a translational alternative: overexpression of p52, the ncNF-κB transcription partner of RELB. Under prolonged antigen exposure, p52 overexpression sustained proliferation, preserved effector functions, and increased the intratumoral trafficking potential, particularly in CD8⁺ T cells, thereby yielding superior tumor control. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated upregulation of cell cycle programs and chemokine receptors, along with downregulation of apoptosis and exhaustion-associated modules. Moreover, p52 overexpression restored RELB nuclear translocation in the context of PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, indicating partial resistance to checkpoint-mediated suppression and sustained ncNF-κB activity in PD-L1hi immunosuppressive environments. Collectively, our findings identify p52 as an antigen-dependent enhancer of ncNF-κB, conferring durable persistence and checkpoint resilience on TCR-based T cells and providing a feasible strategy to improve therapeutic effects in solid tumors.

title: CRISPRa screen unveils noncanonical NF-κB to boost the antitumor activity of TCR-based CAR-T cells.

abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs) coordinate cellular lipid utilization, energy homeostasis, redox balance, and autophagy through dynamic inter-organelle communication with mitochondria. This review summarized recent advances in the molecular mechanisms regulating LD-mitochondria interactions and discusses how their dysregulation contributes to disease progression. Accumulating evidence has indicated that the contacts between LD and mitochondria are dynamically regulated through specialized membrane contact sites and protein complexes, such as Perilipin (PLIN) family of proteins, Mitofusin2 (Mfn2), and Rab GTPases. Rather than being a passive structural association, this interaction serves as a regulatory hub that integrates fatty acid (FA) transport, metabolic adaptation, and stress responses. It enables bidirectional regulation of lipid metabolism, allowing cells to flexibly and efficiently switch between lipid storage and FA oxidation in response to metabolic signals. Disruption of this inter-organelle communication impairs intracellular lipid utilization, compromises mitochondrial function, and exacerbates oxidative stress and ferroptosis. Such dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core mechanism underlying metabolic disorders, cardiovascular diseases and neurodegenerative diseases. In the future, integration of protein regulation, gene editing technologies, and precision therapeutic approaches may enable specific targeting of LD-mitochondria communication, thereby offering new avenues for the treatment of relevant diseases.

title: Mechanisms of Lipid Droplet-Mitochondria Interactions and Their Roles in Diseases.

abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.

title: Dysregulated Metal Homeostasis in Alzheimer's Disease: From Pathological Modulators to Therapeutic Targets.

abstract: Oxidized phospholipids (OxPLs) represent a class of molecules generated during evolution that shift from fundamental membrane building-blocks to key signaling mediators, linking lipid metabolism, cellular redox homeostasis and multi-faceted cell-fate control. Generated by both enzymatic and non-enzymatic peroxidation events, OxPLs engage in extensive signaling crosstalk with lyso-phospholipids and oxylipins. The FerroLipid framework describes iron-lipid peroxidation crosstalk to contextualize iron-dependent lipid signaling. OxPLs govern diverse regulated cell-death programs: they act as lipid death signals in apoptosis and ferroptosis, tune ferroptotic outputs through intrinsic antioxidant systems, and exert context-specific modulatory effects on pyroptosis and other cell-death modalities. Beyond cell-death execution, OxPLs signal through pattern-recognition, scavenger and nuclear receptors to orchestrate inflammation, membrane remodeling, phagocytic clearance, autophagy, mitophagy and protein homeostasis. Threshold-dependent accumulation of OxPLs drives pathological processes across neurodegenerative, metabolic, cardiovascular, neoplastic and infectious diseases; their disease-specific molecular signatures confer potential as both diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Redox phospholipidomics coupled with mass-spectrometry imaging enables accurate, species-resolved profiling of distinct OxPL species. Multiple pharmacological approaches and gene-editing interventions have demonstrated tangible translational prospects for OxPL-oriented therapy. This review synthesizes existing knowledge of OxPL biology from evolutionary origins and signaling mechanisms to disease relevance, analytical tools and therapeutic opportunities. It highlights major unresolved research bottlenecks and provides a solid conceptual foundation for advancing lipid-targeted treatments for complex human disorders.
