title: Oxidized phospholipids: evolution, signaling, cell death, and human diseases.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the fact that immunotherapy is reshaping the therapeutic landscape of bladder cancer, immune evasion remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Therefore, elucidating the mechanisms underlying immune resistance is essential for developing novel therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: In this study, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in bladder cancer cells co-cultured with CD8+ T cells and identified the SLP adaptor and CSK-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) as a key gene that enhances CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity.
RESULTS: SCIMP serves as a favorable prognostic biomarker in patients with bladder cancer treated with immunotherapy. Mechanistically, SCIMP restricts JAK1 phosphorylation in an adaptor-independent manner, suppressing the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT5A/PD-L1 signaling axis. Meanwhile, YTHDF2 destabilizes the m6A-tagged SCIMP transcripts to reduce their expression. Remarkably, SCIMP synergizes with PD-1 blockade in suppressing tumor growth.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unexplored non-canonical role of SCIMP in preventing immune evasion and provide a potential therapeutic target for bladder cancer.

title: Non-canonical function of SCIMP restricts JAK1 activity to counteract immune evasion in bladder cancer.

abstract: Prostate cancers harboring CDK12 alterations exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and poor responses to current therapeutic strategies. Although CDK12 is categorized as a homologous recombination repair (HRR)-related gene, clinical evidence indicates limited benefit of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor monotherapy in CDK12-defective tumors. To clarify the functional consequences of CDK12 loss and identify a mechanistically rational therapeutic approach, we generated CDK12-knockout (KO) prostate cancer cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 and assessed cell-cycle regulation, DNA damage repair, and replication stress via flow cytometry, γH2AX immunofluorescence, and DNA fiber assays. CDK12 KO abrogated the G0-G1 checkpoint, permitting cell-cycle progression into the M-phase despite the persistence of unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSB), and reduced ATM transcription, resulting in a DSB response phenotype resembling ATM deficiency. CDK12 loss also increased intrinsic replication stress and sensitized prostate cancer cells to ATR inhibition. In patient-derived xenograft models harboring CDK12 alterations, combined PARP and ATR inhibition led to enhanced DSB accumulation and selectively suppressed tumor growth in CDK12-defective models. These findings highlight the importance of interrogating individual genes within the HRR pathway to define distinct mechanistic vulnerabilities and provide a strong rationale for combined PARP and ATR inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with CDK12-altered prostate cancer.

abstract: Mitochondria are essential structures that produce energy in cells through mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and are one of the primary sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) cause a wide range of hereditary illnesses with multisystem clinical symptoms, poor cellular bioenergetics, and decreased mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Effective treatment approaches have been hampered by the genetic complexity associated with mtDNA disorders, including heteroplasmy and tissue-specific diversity. The relationship between mutations in the mitochondrial DNA and oxidative stress is multidimensional and snowballing, with structural malfunction of the electron transport chain encouraging the development of ROS that causes further damage to mitochondrial DNA, lipids, and proteins. Under carefully regulated experimental conditions, cell-based disease models, in particular induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and standard transmitochondrial cybrids, have become useful tools for studying disease mechanisms, simulating mutation-specific phenotypes, and assessing possible therapeutic interventions. This review provides the key roles of mutations and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of the disease in the context of the primary role of the mitochondrial genome, its maternal inheritance, and the most common disorders, i.e., mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF). We outline the use of cell-based models to study mitochondrial pathologies, including patient-derived primary cells and iPSCs, which could be differentiated into cell types of interest to the disease, and cybrid systems, which could isolate the contribution of single mutations in the mitochondrial DNA to an underlying background of controlled nuclear genetic backgrounds. Besides, the review focuses on innovative technologies to mend mutations in mitochondrial DNA, such as allotopic expression, mitoTALENs and mitoZFNs, and the new base-editing systems like DdCBEs. Included are the free cell-based therapies like mitochondrial transfer and nuclear transfer procedures. Finally, we discussed the measures to be taken to minimize oxidative stress, and these actions are standard: mitochondria- targeted antioxidants, mitophagy, and autophagy regulation. The study also looks at the present level of proof supporting these therapy techniques and discusses the advantages and disadvantages of existing experimental models. Although several gene editing and mitochondria replacement technologies have shown promising results in clinical and cellular research, their clinical translation is still restricted and needs more confirmation in terms of long-term therapeutic efficacy, safety, and delivery efficiency.

abstract: Articular cartilage repair remains a major clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of the tissue and the poor therapeutic efficacy of current treatments. Although stem cell-based therapies hold promise, their clinical outcomes are often compromised by insufficient chondrogenic differentiation, phenotypic instability, and rapid cell loss in the dynamic joint environment. Herein, we report an ultrasound-responsive, bio-scaffold system (e-BMSCs/Gel) designed to enhance cartilage regeneration through coordinated biochemical and genetic regulation. In this system, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are engineered by internalizing nanobubbles (NBs) loaded with TGF-β3 protein and CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids targeting the YAP (pCas9-YAP), termed T@NBspDNA. Additionally, to enhance cell retention and survival, engineered BMSCs (e-BMSCs) are encapsulated within a thermosensitive thiolated-chitosan/hydroxyapatite hydrogel that rapidly forms in situ. Under US stimulation, the synchronized activation of TGF-β3 release and YAP gene silencing significantly promoted the chondrogenic differentiation of e-BMSCs. Furthermore, in vivo evaluation in a rat articular cartilage defect model demonstrates that US-activated e-BMSCs/Gel effectively promotes hyaline-like cartilage regeneration and improves structural restoration of the defect site. Overall, this work presents a controllable bio-scaffold platform, offering a novel strategy for effective cartilage regeneration.

abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD+. Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD+ from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

abstract: In an extended series of studies, we have shown that Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) has a novel role in regulating opioid signal transduction and antinociception in both the brain and spinal cord. Inhibition in the spinal cord enhances opioid antinociception, which led to the finding that an isoform-selective Hsp90 inhibitor could improve opioid therapy, both enhancing pain relief and reducing side effects. However, the signaling mechanisms for this activity are still not fully understood. We thus identified Dual Specificity Phosphatase 15 (DUSP15) from an earlier proteomic study as a protein enhanced in the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibition. Using male and female CD-1 mice, we confirmed that DUSP15 is upregulated in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibitor (17-AAG) treatment. Using CRISPR and siRNA-mediated knockdown, we showed that DUSP15 was necessary for the enhanced morphine antinociception after Hsp90 inhibitor treatment in both the tail flick and post-surgical paw incision pain models. Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) and behavioral tools, we placed DUSP15 upstream of both ERK MAPK and AMPK in the opioid signaling cascade. We then used IHC to demonstrate that DUSP15 upregulation occurs at least in part in CGRP neurons, and using cell-selective CRISPR, showed that DUSP15 in CGRP neurons is necessary for the enhanced antinociception observed with spinal Hsp90 inhibitor treatment. Together these studies further expand the known mechanisms by which Hsp90 regulates opioid signal transduction and pain relief and provide basic science insight into a potential strategy to improve opioid therapy using Hsp90 inhibitors.

abstract:
Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have substantially extended survival in many patients, most patients do not achieve durable responses on these treatments. There is a substantial unmet need for methods to sensitize more patients to ICIs. Studies have shown that personalized mRNA lipid nanoparticle vaccines enhance antitumor immunity in combination with PD1 inhibition, under the assumption that these vaccines generate T cells reactive against the targets encoded by the mRNA in the vaccines. However, it was recently found that mRNA vaccines targeting non-tumor antigens are also powerful adjuvants to immune checkpoint blockade.

Retrospective clinical data strongly suggests that receipt of COVID mRNA vaccines with ICIs is responsible for significant improvements in three-year overall survival in multiple large cohorts of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Patients treated with these vaccines also have increased expression of programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) on their tumors.

This trial is designed to evaluate whether the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID mRNA vaccine improves responses to ICIs in patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer.

abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Angiotensinogen (AGT) is the precursor of angiotensin peptides and a key determinant of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activity. ART101 is an investigational N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA (GalNAc-siRNA) designed to durably suppress hepatic AGT synthesis.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of single ascending doses of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA in healthy volunteers and to provide an initial exploratory assessment of blood pressure effects in patients with hypertension.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase I study was conducted from January 2025 to April 2026 with 24-week follow-up. Part A was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, single ascending-dose trial; part B was an open-label, single-dose study. The study took place at Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. Part A enrolled 40 healthy adults randomized 6:2 to receive the GalNAc-siRNA (25-600 mg) or placebo; 39 completed the study. Part B enrolled 8 patients with hypertension receiving the GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg; all completed the study.
INTERVENTIONS: A single subcutaneous injection of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA (25, 75, 150, 300, or 600 mg) or placebo in part A; a single open-label subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg, in part B.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes included pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, exploratory blood pressure assessments, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system biomarkers.
RESULTS: Among 40 healthy volunteers (27 [67.5%] male; mean [SD] age, 40.4 [7.8] years) and 8 patients (6 [75.0%] male; mean [SD] age, 47.3 [10.3] years) with hypertension, the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA was well tolerated. In part A, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 23 of 30 active-treatment participants (76.7%) vs 7 of 10 placebo recipients (70.0%); in part B, 6 of 8 patients (75.0%) had TEAEs. No serious adverse events, injection site reactions, or hyperkalemia were observed; all TEAEs were mild to moderate. Plasma exposure (maximum plasma concentration [Cmax] and area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) increased with dose over the wide dose range from 25 mg to 600 mg. Mean maximum serum AGT reductions of 93% (at 600 mg) in healthy volunteers and 90% (at 600 mg) in patients with hypertension were observed. At 24 weeks after a single 600-mg dose, the placebo-corrected 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure decreased by 12.9 mm Hg in healthy participants.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this phase I study, no serious treatment-related safety signals were identified. Sustained, dose-dependent AGT reductions and exploratory blood pressure lowering were observed. These findings support further investigation of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA as a potential long-acting therapeutic for hypertension.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: China Drug Clinical Registry Identifiers: CTR20250041 (part A) and CTR20253973 (part B).

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable remission rates exceeding 80% in relapsed/refractory pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), yet 40-50% of patients eventually relapse within the first year. This therapeutic ceiling is not a single failure mode but the convergence of at least four interrelated layers: loss of CAR-T persistence, antigen escape driven by CD19 splicing variants and lineage switch, CAR-T cell-intrinsic exhaustion from chronic tonic signaling, and an immunosuppressive bone marrow microenvironment that actively extinguishes effector function. Our systematic analysis of 226 pediatric-eligible CAR-T trials shows that 95.6% are Phase I-II, 3.5% (8/226) are registered as Phase III/IV, and 58 of 102 completed trials (56.9%) had no outcome recorded in the source database. In this Perspective, we synthesize the molecular mechanisms of CAR-T resistance, contextualize them within the current clinical trial landscape, and critically evaluate emerging engineering strategies-from dual-targeting and armored CAR architectures to CRISPR-edited allogeneic products and in vivo mRNA delivery. We argue that progress depends on both smarter receptor design and structural reforms in trial design, outcome transparency and global collaboration.

abstract: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

abstract:
This is an open-label, first-in-human, dose escalation study of CV09070101 mRNA (CVHNLC) in patients with metastatic Squamous Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer (sqNSCLC).

The study will evaluate the safety and tolerability of CVHNLC plus pembrolizumab in an Dose Escalation Part and, once the safety of this combination is established, CVHNLC plus prembrolizumab and chemotherapy (carboplatin and paclitaxel) will be evaluated in an Dose Expansion Part with the recommended dose selected from the Dose Escalation Part.
description:
Dose Escalation (Metastatic 1L Maintenance sqNSCLC) The Dose Escalation Part will be comprised of 3 dose cohorts with a starting dose of 100 μg (dose level 1). Once the starting dose is established as safe, further dose levels of 200 μg and 400 μg may be explored. Depending on safety assessment guided by a Bayesian Logistic Regression Model (BLRM) design intermediate dose levels may be explored. In case the HTD is exceeded at 100 μg, a lower dose level of 50 μg may be explored.

Approximately 3 to 6 patients will be enrolled per dose level/cohort. To better understand the safety and tolerability of CVHNLC, additional patients may be enrolled in enrichment cohorts at dose levels that have previously been determined to be safe in at least 3 patients. This may be before or while proceeding with the next higher dose. An enrichment cohort may have up to 10 patients enrolled.

Each dose level will start with the staggered enrollment of 3 patients. There will be a 2-week interval between the first CVHNLC administration of the first patient and the first CVHNLC administration of the second patient. The same approach will be used between the second and third patient. If the cohort is enriched with further patients, subsequent patients may be treated concurrently once the second patient has completed the 2 weeks after the first CVHNLC administration. The enrollment is followed by a safety data review by the Safety Review Team (SRT) after all patients in each cohort have completed their 4 weeks DLT evaluation period. Non-evaluable patients (patients that discontinue/withdraw during the DLT assessment period for a reason other than DLT) may be replaced.

Safety will be continuously monitored by the Sponsor's Safety Physician, Sponsor's Medical Responsible Person (MRP) and the medical monitor with a focus on DLTs, Grade ≥ 3 AEs occurring after the DLT period, SAEs, and AESIs. After completion of the DLT evaluation period in all patients enrolled in a dose cohort, the SRT will review the safety data from the respective and all previous dose cohorts together with the Coordinating Investigator and decide about the next steps e.g.:

* Escalation of the dose to the next level.
* Enrollment of additional patients at the same or lower dose level.
* Stop or pause enrollment in the Dose Escalation Part of the trial.

At the end of the Dose Escalation Part, an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) will recommend a dose for the Dose Expansion Part (RDE) based on review of the complete safety data from the Dose Escalation Part and the Sponsor will decide on the RDE.

Dose Expansion Part (Metastatic 1L sqNSCLC) The optional Dose Expansion Part will include patients with histologically confirmed metastatic sqNSCLC not amenable for surgical or locoregional therapy and eligible for 1L treatment with pembrolizumab and platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin/paclitaxel). Patients should not have received any prior systemic treatment for metastatic disease. Previous (neo-)adjuvant treatment is only permitted if there are at least 12 months between end of such treatment and development of metastatic disease. Patients will receive CVHNLC plus 4 cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel and pembrolizumab (3-weekly) followed by pembrolizumab maintenance therapy. Patients who discontinue prematurely from chemotherapy due to toxicity may continue on CVHNLC plus pembrolizumab. The first dose of CVHNLC will be administered one week prior to chemotherapy to avoid the immune suppressive effect from concomitant administration of steroids as premedication/supportive medication to chemotherapy treatment. Once chemotherapy is completed, CVHNLC administration will be aligned with pembrolizumab treatment to reduce patient visit burden.

The Dose Expansion Part will start with a safety lead-in, where the first 6 patients will be evaluated with focus on treatment-related AEs, SAEs, and AESIs after having completed the Day 29 visit, before continuing the enrollment. The safety data will be reviewed by the SRT and in addition by the DSMB, which will give a recommendation on dosage for treatment continuation. Patients will receive CVHNLC plus pembrolizumab for up to 12 months or until disease progression or undue toxicity. Patients not progressing after this period may continue on pembrolizumab outside of the trial according to standard of care.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics represent a transformative pharmacological paradigm in which the delivery vehicle, genetic payload, and expressed protein form a tightly coupled system. This multicomponent structure introduces nonlinear, multiscale dynamics that challenge traditional pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic frameworks, making quantitative modeling essential.
AREAS COVERED: This review provides a structured biological framework for mRNA-LNP therapeutics, detailing the key processes governing delivery, endosomal escape, mRNA stability, and translation, and highlighting their associated temporal and spatial scales, providing the key aspects to consider for modeling. Building on this foundation, we summarize mathematical modeling approaches, including pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK), and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, used to represent these mechanisms. The literature was surveyed to identify representative preclinical and translational studies, focusing on model structure, assumptions, and their use in human projection and dose optimization.
EXPERT OPINION: Mathematical models are increasingly critical to interpret and predict mRNA therapeutic behavior, yet challenges remain in parameter identifiability, data availability, and model standardization. Future advances will depend on biologically grounded modeling frameworks, improved integration of mechanistic insight with quantitative approaches, and tighter coupling between experimental design and model development. These developments will support more efficient translation and enable precision medicine applications.

abstract: Skin fibrosis is driven in part by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling and the matricellular protein connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). Elevated CTGF expression is a hallmark of fibrotic skin lesions and contributes to pathological extracellular matrix remodeling. In this project, an antisense oligonucleotide (AON) delivery system was developed for the treatment of skin fibrosis. In this respect, two antifibrotic agents, i) AON against CTGF and ii) antifibrotic polypeptide amphiphile, were self-assembled into nanofibers to enhance antifibrotic efficacy. The nanofibers were encapsulated in chitosan nanoparticles (CNPs) for protection and sustained release. Loaded CNPs were characterized by morphology, size, endosomal escape, and skin penetration using a transwell-based 3D skin model. The nanoparticles exhibited an average size of 220 nm. The encapsulation efficiency of CNPs was 52%, providing sustained nanofiber release over 7 days. With the use of nanoparticles, clear reduction trends were observed in CTGF, α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA), and collagen expression. CNPs penetrated the skin model gradually, revealing no cytotoxicity to skin cells. Overall, these results reveal the potential of the designed nanofibers as a therapeutic agent and the CNPs as the carrier of the nanofibers. The developed delivery system can be used as an alternative approach for the treatment of lesions in fibrotic skin.

abstract: Secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (SFRP2) is an important molecule that regulates cell growth and development and participates in hair follicle (HF) development and homeostasis. The present study seeks to determine whether SFRP2 directly targets dermal papilla cells (DPCs), the pivotal functional cell population within HF, and characterize the intracellular signaling regulatory network triggered downstream. In this study, a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SFRP2 gene editing DPC model was established in vitro. Multi-omics analyses, including transcriptomics and metabolomics, were performed alongside functional assays to investigate the regulatory mechanisms of SFRP2 in DPCs. Among three designed single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), sgRNA3 showed the highest editing efficiency (67.0%) without off-target effects. Genetic editing of SFRP2 markedly increased the transcript levels of pivotal hair follicle‑development‑related genes (LEF1, CCND1 and Wnt2). Meanwhile, it suppressed TGF‑β1 transcription, which resulted in elevated proliferation capacity and diminished apoptotic activity within DPCs. Transcriptomic profiling identified 2288 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in PI3K-Akt, MAPK and TNF signaling pathways, while metabolomic analysis identified 185 differential metabolites (DMs) associated with apoptosis, ABC transporters, and PI3K-Akt signaling. Integrated multi-omics analysis confirmed PI3K-Akt signaling as a central regulatory axis. Western blot analysis revealed increased phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt following SFRP2 editing, indicating pathway activation. Treatment of SFRP2-edited DPCs with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reduced the elevated phosphorylation and reversed the functional phenotypes, confirming PI3K-Akt pathway involvement. Collectively, these findings indicate that SFRP2 mediates DPC biological activities by means of PI3K‑Akt‑driven transcriptional‑metabolic networks, yielding novel perspectives on the molecular regulatory machinery controlling HF physiology.

abstract: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy, and effective gene therapy remains limited by ocular barriers, tumor heterogeneity, and inefficient nucleic acid delivery. This review critically analyses the molecular rationale, engineering principles, emerging nanoarchitectures, biological validation, and translational prospects of dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma. The manuscript also highlights key challenges and future strategies for clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that dual-vector platforms enable independent optimization of mRNA and CRISPR cargos while maintaining coordinated spatiotemporal therapeutic activity. We conducted a literature search in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for relevant studies published from January 2015 to September 2026. Functional cargo partitioning, vector modularity, programmable intracellular trafficking, and ocular-targeted nanoengineering improve delivery precision and reduce biological compromise associated with co-encapsulation. Lipid, polymeric, hybrid, biomimetic, and viral-nonviral architectures each provide distinct engineering advantages depending on therapeutic objectives. Preclinical studies support enhanced genome editing, transient protein restoration, improved tumor suppression, and reduced off-target effects. Nevertheless, manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, long-term safety, and clinical validation remain major barriers to translation. Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR systems represent a promising next-generation platform for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma by enabling coordinated and programmable therapeutic delivery. Continued advances in modular nanoengineering, personalized cargo selection, and clinically scalable manufacturing will be essential for successful translation into precision ocular oncology.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies. Dysregulated RNA splicing has emerged as a critical mechanism contributing to PDAC progression. However, whether structural components of the spliceosome regulate oncogenic alternative splicing was not known. Here, we identify the nineteen complex (NTC) component BCAS2/SPF27 as a critical regulator of PDAC progression. Elevated expression of BCAS2 in PDAC is associated with poor patient outcomes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that BCAS2 specifically regulates alternative exons with weak splice sites. In particular, BCAS2 promotes SOS1 exon 21 inclusion and consequently RAC-signaling activation. Furthermore, splice-switching antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated skipping of SOS1 exon 21 suppressed PDAC proliferation and migration. Our findings uncover a role of BCAS2 in the regulation of weak splice-site usage and identify the BCAS2-SOS1-RAC signaling axis as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

abstract: Cellular and gene-based therapies are being investigated as potential strategies to address current treatment limitations in breast cancer. Adoptive cell therapies, such as CAR-T, TCR-T, TILs and NK cell-based therapies, are currently under investigation for their ability to selectively target tumor-associated antigens. Also, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing is being investigated as a strategy to enhance T cell persistence, improve tumor infiltration, and increase resistance to immunosuppressive signaling. Although cellular and gene-based therapies have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, their application in breast cancer remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, immune exclusion, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Among current approaches, TIL-based therapies have provided some of the clearest evidence of clinical activity selected patients, whereas the clinical efficacy of CAR-T and gene-editing strategies as standalone interventions remains uncertain. Future progress may depend on biomarker-guided, combinatorial approaches rather than single-modality therapies. This review examines the current applications, clinical evidence, and limitations of these approaches in breast cancer.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and muscle wasting. Exon skipping therapies have been approved as part of the therapeutic arsenal for DMD, however, there is contrasting evidence regarding their clinical benefits. The aim of this study was to determine the efficacy and safety of exon skipping therapies for DMD.
METHOD: ology: A systematic review was conducted in three databases including PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Cochrane-Ovid, based on the following question using PICO strategy: What is the efficacy of exon skipping therapies for DMD? Search was limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and Open Label RCTs with reported results, published between January 2016 and December 2024, involving patients with DMD treated with any of the existing exon-skipping therapies, reporting efficacy measured by primary clinical and secondary molecular outcomes. Secondary safety outcomes were also registered. Eligible studies were assessed for risk of bias. A descriptive analysis was performed in subgroups according to variants amenable to exon 45, 51, or 53 skipping.
RESULTS: A total of nine studies were left after the final filters were applied. Studies were conducted across centers in seven different countries. Four studies used viltolarsen (exon 53), three eteplirsen (exon 51), and two golodirsen (exon 53). Trial length was heterogeneous with an average length of 119.6 weeks (±78.5). Overall, studies with exon skipping medications reported improvement in the clinical outcomes including the 6-minute walking test, time to stand and the North Star Ambulatory Assessment. Biological measurements showed an increase in dystrophin expression and exon skipping percentage. Long term follow up evidenced stabilization of both clinical and molecular outcomes in DMD patients, compared to age and treatment-matched controls.
CONCLUSION: Exon skipping therapies have evidenced improved clinical and molecular outcomes. Longer follow-up extension studies are needed to further elucidate their effect in comparison to age-matched controls.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the most severe global health threats. The rapid expansion of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) pathogens compromises the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics. Globally, ESKAPE organisms (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) have led to therapeutic failure, prolonged hospitalization, and increased mortality rates. This review identifies the molecular mechanisms, including enzymatic antibiotic inactivation, efflux pump overexpression, biofilm formation, and horizontal gene transfer, that underline the resistance of disseminated pathogens to antibiotics in clinical, agricultural, and environmental settings. Antibiotic overuse and pharmaceutical and agricultural discharges create persistent reservoirs for the dissemination of AMR genes. Furthermore, we evaluated the non-traditional antibacterial efficacy of antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage therapy, monoclonal antibodies, probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, anti-virulence agents, CRISPR-Cas precision antimicrobials, and nanotechnology-based drug delivery platforms. Current preclinical and clinical evidence indicates the eradication of resistant pathogens, disruption of biofilms, and preservation of host microbiota, thereby reducing the selective pressure associated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Despite these advances, major translational barriers, such as pharmacokinetic instability, manufacturing limitations, and insufficient clinical validation, restrict the implementation of the framework. In the future, the AMR management framework will require precision medicine, artificial intelligence, and One Health-based integration via multidisciplinary collaboration.

title: Combating Antimicrobial Resistance: Emerging Non-Traditional Therapeutics, Clinical Translation Challenges, and Future Perspectives.

abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.

title: Molecular insights into the long terminal repeat regions of therapeutic staphylococcal Twortvirinae phages.

abstract: Efficient engineering of human and murine primary T cells without perturbation of cellular function is crucial for immunotherapy and immunology research. Here, we present a protocol for genome editing of primary T cells with minimal toxicity using peptide-assisted genome editing. We describe key steps required for primary T cell isolation and activation, CRISPR ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly and delivery mediated by peptide, and assessment of editing efficiency. This protocol maintains T cell proliferative capacity and functional potency. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zhang et al.1.

title: Protocol for engineering primary human and mouse T cells using peptide-assisted genome editing.

abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.

title: Targeting phenol-soluble modulins: eco-friendly theragnostic strategies against Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Seasonal influenza epidemics cause significant mortality, especially among the elderly. Influenza A virus triggers the host innate immune system through various mechanisms. Human enzymes belonging to the group of RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADARs) play a role in the innate antiviral immune response, partly by inducing mutations in viral RNA. The effect of this mechanismin influenza A virus infection remains unexplained in humans.
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess the clinical impact of ADAR-induced mutations on influenza A virus in hospitalised patients.
METHODS: Full-genome deep sequencing of Influenza A virus was performed on respiratory samples from 75 hospitalised, Influenza A(H3N2) virus infected patients, aged 41 to 95 years. ADAR-associated mutations in minor viral subpopulations were analysed in relation to demographic and clinical factors.
RESULTS: ADAR-associated mutations showed a significant inverse correlation with viral load (p < 0.0001) and age (p = 0.0051), especially in patients older than 75 years. The association between ADAR-associated mutations and viral load was independent of age, inflammation, and disease severity (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: We found an association between ADAR-induced mutations and viral load, which may indicate an antiviral function of ADAR on influenza A virus. The lower mutation rate and associated higher viral load in the elderly suggest an age-dependent reduced ADAR activity, which may contribute to increased disease severity.

abstract: Chemical conjugation can modulate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) pharmacology and improve organ-specific delivery, yet whole-tissue measurements provide limited information on cell-specific activity. Here, we used metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (Malat1) knockdown as a pharmacodynamic readout to compare whole-tissue and cell-resolved activity of chemically conjugated ASOs in platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha-enhanced green fluorescent protein (PDGFR-eGFP) mouse model to assess their in vivo uptake in PDGFR-expressing (GFP+) cells. This reporter mouse model uses PDGFR as an exemplar cellular marker and provides an accessible tool for evaluating ASO conjugate activity within mesenchymal stromal and progenitor populations, mainly tissue fibroblasts. Following subcutaneous administration, Malat1 was quantified in whole tissues and cell-sorted PDGFR+/GFP or PDGFR-/GFP- populations. ASO-mediated Malat1 reduction varied by tissue and conjugate chemistry, with palmitate conjugation producing the broadest extrahepatic activity and pronounced whole-tissue activity in heart and skeletal muscle. Cell-resolved analysis further revealed preferential palmitate-ASO activity within PDGFR skeletal-muscle populations. Preliminary safety assessment also showed conjugate-dependent differences, with body-weight loss and ALT elevation in tocopherol-ASO-treated male mice and spleen enlargement in both sexes. These findings present an in vivo modelling system for evaluating cell-specific ASO activity and demonstrate the advantages of cell-resolved assessment over whole-tissue measurements.

abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold immense therapeutic potential, yet their clinical translation is hindered by nonspecific cellular uptake and the complexity and cost of surface engineering. Here, we present the EZON (Easy OligoNucleotide) EV modification platform, a cost-effective, post-isolation modification system that addresses both limitations simultaneously. The EZON platform employs unmodified DNA aptamers that bind directly to tetraspanin proteins on EV surfaces, eliminating the need for cholesterol conjugation, covalent chemistry, or genetic engineering of producer cells. EVs are thus easily and rapidly functionalized in a single incubation step at substantially reduced oligonucleotide cost. The EZON platform enables dual functionality: (1) the oligonucleotide anchor (ONA) sequence inhibits nonspecific cellular uptake, while (2) the display strand enables targeted delivery through ligand-mediated internalization. We demonstrate that our optimized ONA construct efficiently functionalizes EVs from multiple mammalian cell types. Cancer cells selectively internalized EZON-modified EVs functionalized with AS1411, an aptamer that targets nucleolin, whereas off-target internalization was suppressed. The platform's versatility extends to protein display via histidine-tag aptamers and therapeutic cargo delivery, as demonstrated by targeted doxorubicin delivery to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells. This rapid, modular approach transforms unmodified EVs into precision delivery vehicles within hours, offering a scalable solution for targeted therapeutics.

abstract: CIRV2 is a Phase IV randomized, open-label, trial of FDA-approved COVID-19 and/or influenza vaccines (no more than minimal risk) with longitudinal follow-up. In 2026 CIRV2 will compare immunogenicity and reactogenicity of the recombinant Novavax COVID-19 vaccine and the mRNA Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine.

outcomes.description: The primary endpoint is variant-specific immune response (magnitude and breadth) to licensed recombinant and mRNA COVID-19 products administered to adult MHS beneficiaries who are eligible for a fall COVID-19 vaccine and who are not severely immunocompromised. This will include quantifying the magnitude of binding and neutralizing antibodies to the vaccine variants and to the dominant variant present 30 days and 150 days post-vaccination. Specifically, we will test neutralizing titers (defined as the inverse serum dilution causing a 50% reduction in relative light units in a pseudovirus neutralization assay) and IgG binding antibody levels (measured in arbitrary units) against the following SARS-CoV-2 variants: XFG (vaccine strain), Wuhan-1 (ancestral strain), plus the dominant circulating variant(s) circulating during the fall of 2026 and winter of 2026-2027.
outcomes.measure: Variant-specific immune responses (Year 2 Only)
outcomes.time_frame: IgG binding antibody levels and neutralizing antibody titers will be assessed on serum samples obtained just prior to vaccination, 30 days (+/- 10 days), and 150 days (+/- 10 days) after vaccination.

outcomes.description: The primary endpoint is variant-specific immune response (magnitude and breadth) to licensed recombinant and mRNA COVID-19 products administered to healthy adult MHS beneficiaries. This will include quantifying the magnitude of binding and neutralizing antibodies to the vaccine variants and to the dominant variant present one month post-vaccination. Specifically, we will test neutralizing titers (defined as the inverse serum dilution causing a 50% reduction in relative light units in a pseudovirus neutralization assay) and IgG binding antibody levels (measured in arbitrary units) against the following SARS-CoV-2 variants: NB.1.8.1 and XFG (predominant circulating strains in fall 2025), JN.1 and LP.8.1 (vaccine strains), and Wuhan-1 (ancestral strain).
outcomes.measure: Variant-specific immune responses (Year 1 Only)
outcomes.time_frame: IgG binding antibody levels and neutralizing antibody titers will be assessed on serum samples obtained just prior to vaccination and 30 days (+/- 10 days after vaccination).

outcomes.description: For vaccine reactogenicity and other incident adverse events, we will use Fisher exact test or a Chi-square test between study arms. Any comparisons among substrata (e.g., age strata, infection histories) will use multiplicity adjustment.
outcomes.measure: Vaccine reactogenicity and other incident adverse events (compared between two licensed COVID-19 platforms - recombinant and mRNA)
outcomes.time_frame: Reactogenicity and other incident adverse events will be assessed through 9 months after vaccination.

outcomes.description: Salivary and nasopharyngeal IgG and IgA antibody levels to vaccine SARS-CoV-2 strain and dominant SARS-CoV-2 circulating strain at 30 days and 5 months post vaccination will be compared between the study arms using GMT and GSD. T-tests will compare responses across two SARS-CoV-2 variants (i.e., the vaccine variant and the dominant circulating variant at the time of vaccination), stratified by vaccine type and adjusted for multiple comparisons (e.g., a Tukey's adjustment). A non-parametric comparison can be used if there is non-normally distributed data despite the use of GMT, these approaches also account for multiplicity (e.g., Kruskall-Wallis with a Dunn's adjustment for multiplicity adjustment).
outcomes.measure: Salivary and nasopharyngeal IgG and IgA antibody levels to vaccine SARS-CoV-2 strain and dominant SARS-CoV-2 circulating strain at 30 days and 5 months post vaccination
outcomes.time_frame: These antibody tests will be conducted on biosamples obtained just prior to vaccination and 30 days (+/- 10 days) and 5 months (+/- 10 days) after vaccination.

outcomes.description: Antigenic cartography and antibody landscapes may be performed by FDA collaborators to visualize antigenic drift from the vaccine with sequential variants, leveraging prior analysis approaches used by the study team. These analyses use relative differences in neutralizing antibody responses to generate two-dimensional maps (antigenic cartography) or three-dimensional landscapes that enable one to assess how antigenically similar different virus strains are to each other. Antibody landscapes are useful tools which can capture differential multiple serial antigenic exposures in comparisons of antibody titer and breadth between individuals assigned to receive the recombinant or mRNA vaccines (see examples from Wang et al., Cell Host Microbe, 2022).
outcomes.measure: Antigenic cartography and antibody landscapes
outcomes.time_frame: Antigenic cartography studies may be conducted using neutralizing antibody titers obtained just prior to vaccination and 30 days (+/- 10 days) after vaccination.

title: Nucleic acid-based and small-molecule therapies for lipoprotein(a) lowering: what the trials teach us and what they do not.

abstract: Phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) enter cells, but their site of productive escape remains uncertain. We combined live-cell imaging and ratiometric pH measurements to follow a Malat1-targeting ASO internalized without a delivery vehicle. In U2OS cells, less than 4% of internalized ASO reached the nucleus under conditions that reduced Malat1 RNA by >90%. Most ASO accumulated in late endosomes, endolysosomes and lysosomes as foci and broadly distributed luminal signal. These compartments underwent neutralization without detectable membrane rupture or galectin-3 recruitment. ASO foci showed constrained motion, consistent with association with endolysosomal constituents. L-leucyl-L-leucine methyl ester-induced membrane damage or Calcium dependent lysosome exocytosis released dextran while retaining luminal ASO. Loss of the stress-granule scaffolding proteins G3BP1/2 modestly enhanced ASO activity without detectable endolysosomal damage. Tantalosin, a small molecule that perturbs endosomal recycling, redistributed the ESCRT-III protein IST1 to endosomes. It enhanced early escape of SYTOX Green and ASOs, detected by nuclear accumulation, and increased Malat1 knockdown, with cell-type-dependent responses. Tantalosin did not detectably increase nuclear ASO accumulation after sequestration in late compartments. These findings place productive ASO escape early in endocytic trafficking, most likely in early or recycling endosomes, before sequestration in largely nonproductive late compartments.

abstract: This is a prospective, multicenter, phase I/II, open-label, two-stage design of PD1+ TILs infusion in metastatic or advanced TNBC. TILS001 includes 3 parts. description: This trial has been developed in TNBC, a breast cancer subtype with a particularly poor prognosis. Finally, NUMARZU-001 will be administered if the patient is eligible for part three of the protocol.

abstract:
The Investigators have demonstrated in preclinical studies that RNA liposomes activate APCs, induce antigen-specific T cell immunity, and can supplant DCs in a cell therapy model for HGG and have shown feasibility and activity of this approach in preclinical models and in canine patients with a spontaneous malignant glioma. In one arm of this study, we will investigate the safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccines in pediatric patients with recurrent pHGG.

The investigators have also shown that intravenous administration of tumor mRNA loaded lipid particles (LPs) localizes primarily to lung, transfect antigen presenting cells (APCs) and lead to an activated T cell response for induction of anti-tumor immunity. In contrast to other formulations, RNA-LPs recruit multiple arms of the immune system (i.e. innate/adaptive), and remodel the systemic/intratumoral immune milieu, which remain potent barriers for vaccine, cellular, and checkpoint inhibiting immunotherapies. After only a single RNA-LP vaccine, the bulk of systemic and intratumoral dendritic cells (DCs) in mice display an activated phenotype; these activated DCs (harvested from tumors) expand antigen specific T cell immunity. In immunologically resistant pulmonary osteosacroma murine tumor models (i.e. K7M2), RNA-LPs induce robust anti-tumor efficacy in settings where immune checkpoint inhibitors (i.e. anti-PD-L1 therapy) do not confer therapeutic benefit. The investigators have already demonstrated safety of RNA-LPs in acute/chronic murine toxicity studies, and in client-owned canine trial.

In this study, we will investigate the manufacturing feasibility, safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccine in patients with recurrent pulmonary or unresectable osteosarcoma and recurrent pHGG.

abstract: Dentin is the primary mineralized tissue of the tooth, essential for pulp protection and enamel support. Its regenerative capacity is critical for dental health. This review summarizes recent progress in odontogenic regeneration, covering fundamental biological mechanisms and translational applications. A literature search of peer-reviewed studies on odontogenic regeneration, dental tissue engineering, and biomaterial-based strategies was conducted. Key advances include signaling pathway-guided stem cell differentiation into functional odontoblasts, which promotes reparative dentin matrix formation, and biomaterial innovations that provide optimized cellular microenvironments. Emerging clinical strategies, including 3D printing, growth factor delivery systems, and gene-editing approaches, are also discussed. Despite substantial progress, challenges remain in the precise control of stem cell fate specification, long-term biocompatibility of biomaterials, and high clinical costs. Future interdisciplinary integration holds promise for overcoming these hurdles, advancing personalized therapies, and expanding dental restoration and regenerative medicine. The evolving strategies offer meaningful potential for dentin-pulp complex regeneration, improved pulp preservation, personalized scaffold fabrication via 3D printing, and the eventual development of cost-effective, biocompatible clinical therapies.

abstract: This review examines the expanding role of PARP inhibitors in cancer therapy, moving beyond the traditional model of single-strand break repair inhibition and BRCA-dependent synthetic lethality. We highlight emerging evidence that PARP inhibitors induce cytotoxicity through replication-associated DNA damage, including defects in Okazaki fragment maturation and replication gap accumulation. By integrating recent mechanistic insights with findings from CRISPR-based screens, we outline how disruptions in DNA replication and repair pathways define a broader BRCAness phenotype. We further emphasize the clinical implications of these discoveries, including novel combination strategies that extend the therapeutic applicability of PARP inhibitors beyond prevailing treatment regimens.

abstract: Fungal keratitis (FK) remains a major cause of vision-threatening corneal infection, especially in tropical and subtropical regions, with an expanding epidemiological spectrum driven by environmental, climatic, occupational and host-related factors. Fusarium and Aspergillus were the most common pathogens reported. Greater etiological diversity is reflected by increasing recognition of dematiaceous fungi, uncommon molds, and cryptic species. The literature search was performed by searching bibliographic databases (PubMed and Google Scholar), covering publications from January 2000 to August 2026. Additional relevant studies were identified by screening the reference lists of key publications. This review provides an overview of the current state of FK including changing epidemiology, established diagnostic approaches, emerging technologies, and evolving therapeutic approaches. Conventional microscopy and culture remain central to diagnosis, with molecular methods, sequencing, MALDI-TOF and noninvasive imaging offering advantages in sensitivity, speed and species-level identification. Novel diagnostic methods such as CRISPR-based tests, genome sequencing, artificial intelligence, biosensors and point-of-care diagnostics may provide rapid and accessible precision diagnosis. Therapeutic challenges include poor corneal drug penetration, antifungal resistance and prolonged treatment. Hence, the exploration of new antifungals, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, photoactivated therapies and antimicrobial peptides. These advances support a transition to integrated, rapid and precision-based management of FK collectively.

abstract: Periodontitis is a common chronic inflammatory disease driven by pathogenic biofilms, leading to progressive periodontal tissue destruction and systemic health risks. Conventional therapies often fail to eradicate biofilms in deep periodontal pockets, promote antimicrobial resistance and offer limited regenerative potential. Although SDT has emerged as a promising alternative, its clinical efficacy is constrained by several material- and microenvironment-related barriers that have not been systematically addressed in previous reviews. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) employs low-intensity ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inducing mechanical disruption of biofilms, with advantages of deep tissue penetration, broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and low risk of resistance. Nevertheless, conventional sonosensitizers often exhibit poor water solubility, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and suboptimal ROS generation, while hypoxia, continuous fluid turnover, and mechanical disturbance within periodontal pockets further compromise local retention and therapeutic efficacy. Advances in biomaterials address these barriers by engineering high-performance sonosensitizers to enhance ROS efficiency, developing delivery systems to improve solubility and prolonged retention and integrating multimodal antibacterial and regenerative functions. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of SDT with recent advances in sonosensitizer engineering, local delivery platforms, synergistic therapies, and multifunctional biomaterials, thereby linking antimicrobial performance to periodontal tissue regeneration. We further identify hypoxia, delivery efficiency, biosafety and the lack of standardized evaluation as key translational challenges, and propose future directions including AI-guided sonosensitizer design, precision delivery systems, and CRISPR-assisted antimicrobial combination strategies to accelerate the clinical translation of SDT for periodontitis management.

abstract: This issue of the Biomedical Journal explores therapeutic approaches to neuroinflammation, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer, as well as developments in laboratory testing and prognostic assessment. Experimental findings show that glibenclamide attenuates palmitic acid-induced hippocampal inflammation and memory impairment in mice. In antimicrobial research, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated elimination of resistance genes restores ertapenem susceptibility in resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, while deep learning offers an approach to interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility tests from images. Oncology articles span molecular characterization, treatment, and prognosis: BK polyomavirus integration and aristolochic acid exposure are associated with distinct molecular features in kidney transplant-associated urothelial carcinomas; bavachinin enhances cisplatin's antitumor activity in oral cancer models; biomarker changes inform prognosis during radium-223 therapy; and external validation supports the MAGIC-D model in advanced biliary tract cancer. Furthermore, research on cartilage homeostasis examines exercise-dependent responses of Prg4-expressing cells. Correspondence addresses combined radiotherapy and systemic treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma and, in a second exchange, stewardship of short-term systemic corticosteroid use.

abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) poses a major public health threat due to high mortality and limited therapeutic options. Rapid and accurate detection of both species identity and resistance determinants is critical for clinical management. Here, we developed a dual-target recombinase polymerase amplification-CRISPR/Cas12a multiplex lateral flow assay (DRC-MLFA) for simultaneous detection of K. pneumoniae and blaKPC in a single reaction. This platform introduces a functionally differentiated dual-channel detection strategy, in which the K. pneumoniae signal is generated directly via RPA-lateral flow readout, while blaKPC detection is achieved through an additional CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated verification step. To enable one-pot integration, suboptimal protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences were employed to delay Cas12a activation, thereby coordinating amplification and CRISPR detection within a single reaction system. Under optimized conditions, the assay achieved dual-target detection within 50 min at 37 °C, with a limit of detection of 101 CFU/μL and high specificity against non-target pathogens. Validation with 30 clinical samples showed strong concordance with quantitative PCR. This portable and low-cost biosensor provides a practical solution for point-of-care detection of CRKP and establishes a framework for integrating hierarchical specificity control into multiplex CRISPR diagnostics.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tendon injuries heal through disorganized extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition rather than the restoration of native collagen architecture, thus resulting in suboptimal functional recovery. Although adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) are attractive for tendon regeneration because of their accessibility and expandability, their tenogenic differentiation efficiency is lower than that of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs). C1q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3) is an adipokine implicated in ECM remodeling and fibrosis; however, its role in tendon lineage regulation is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: CTRP3 (C1q/TNF-related protein 3) contributes to extracellular-matrix remodeling and, in tendon, is associated with a pathological fibrotic matrix signature; we therefore reasoned that reducing CTRP3 would favor a more mature tendon-like matrix. Using a loss-of-function approach based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), we investigated whether CTRP3 disruption alters tenogenic marker expression, at both the transcript and protein levels, and the tendon-associated ECM marker profile of canine ADSCs relative to wild-type ADSCs and native TDSCs.
METHODS: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs were generated and validated using sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting. Wild-type ADSCs, CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs, and TDSCs were subjected to tenogenic induction for 0-3 weeks. Tenogenic transcriptional and ECM markers were analyzed at mRNA and protein levels.
RESULTS: CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs showed increased collagen type I and tenomodulin (TNMD) expression during tenogenic induction compared with wild-type ADSCs. COL III expression showed a transient increase followed by a decline, with lower expression in CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs than in WT cADSCs at week 2. CTRP3 disruption increased early Mkx and Scx expression at the earliest time points but did not consistently alter the early transcriptional program, which rose comparably across all groups. CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs showed partial, marker- and time-point-dependent overlap with native cTDSCs, mainly for selected late ECM markers rather than across the overall transcript and protein profiles.
CONCLUSION: CTRP3 disruption shifted the tendon-associated ECM marker profile during the tenogenic differentiation of ADSCs, with reduced COL III accumulation, rather than uniformly enhancing tenogenic differentiation. Although early transcriptional changes were observed, the more consistent differences were found in late tendon-associated ECM markers. The modulation of CTRP3 may represent a candidate strategy worth further investigation for stem cell-based tendon regeneration in veterinary medicine.

abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. Mitochondrial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration via energy exhaustion, aggravated oxidative stress, pathological protein aggregation and excessive neuronal apoptosis. We further recapitulate mitochondrial‑oriented therapeutic approaches including small‑molecule regulators, mitophagy activators, mitochondrial biogenesis promoters, gene‑editing strategies and mitochondrial transplantation. Notable translational obstacles remain, including limited blood‑brain‑barrier penetration of candidate drugs, narrow therapeutic time‑window post‑symptom onset, and prominent disease heterogeneity. By synthesizing basic experimental findings and pre‑clinical and clinical trial progress, this review provides updated insights into the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and facilitates the development of precise mitochondrial‑targeted therapeutic regimens.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Hypertension remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet blood pressure control rates remain suboptimal despite the widespread availability of effective antihypertensive therapies. Poor long-term adherence, therapeutic inertia, and the need for lifelong daily treatment continue to limit the effectiveness of current pharmacological strategies. This review examines the biological rationale, available clinical evidence, and potential role of long-acting RNA-based therapies targeting hepatic angiotensinogen synthesis in hypertension.
RECENT FINDINGS: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting angiotensinogen represent a novel therapeutic approach that suppresses production of the unique precursor of the renin-angiotensin system. Zilebesiran has demonstrated sustained reductions in circulating angiotensinogen and ambulatory blood pressure following infrequent subcutaneous administration in phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials. Antisense strategies have provided additional clinical validation of sustained angiotensinogen inhibition, although their antihypertensive efficacy has been less consistent. Ongoing clinical development is addressing long-term cardiovascular outcomes, safety, and optimal patient selection. RNA-based antihypertensive therapies may represent an important evolution in hypertension management by combining upstream renin-angiotensin system inhibition with prolonged pharmacological activity and reduced dependence on daily medication adherence. However, their future clinical role will depend on evidence regarding long-term safety, cardiovascular outcomes, reversibility, cost-effectiveness, patient selection, and integration with conventional antihypertensive therapy.

abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

abstract: Reliable assessment of disease status and therapeutic response in osteosarcoma remains an unmet clinical need. Integrative bioinformatics analysis and protein-level verification in paired clinical specimens prioritized secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1, osteopontin) as a liquid biopsy target associated with osteosarcoma progression and patient survival. On this basis, CRUMP, a CRISPR-Cas12a and FUSE Probe-based dual-mode biosensing platform, was developed for SPP1 quantification. A bifunctional NH2-ZIF-8 probe co-immobilizes the components required for target recognition and Cas12a activation, while MoS2@AuNPs interfaces transduce the resulting signals. Signal amplification is achieved through a unipoint-anchored multisite cascade based on a DNA tetrahedron-HCR architecture, enabling one-to-multiple parallel amplification while balancing stability and sensitivity. A single Cas12a cleavage event simultaneously decreases the electrochemical (EC) signal and increases the fluorescence (FL) signal. These reciprocal changes allow the two readouts to provide an internal consistency check for each measurement. Each channel covers more than five orders of magnitude, with detection limits of 167.7 fg/mL for EC and 331.6 fg/mL for FL. The broad measurement ranges allow most serum samples to be analyzed directly, without the per-sample dilution optimization that ELISA requires, and the complete analysis takes only approximately 85 min. Validation across osteosarcoma cell lines, clinical specimens, and tumor-bearing mouse models provided preliminary evidence for the feasibility of CRUMP in SPP1 quantification and endpoint assessment of chemotherapeutic response. By combining biomarker prioritization, biosensor engineering, and preliminary application testing, this work presents CRUMP as a candidate platform for SPP1-based assessment of osteosarcoma and its therapeutic response.

abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, causes a connected spectrum of pharyngeal, cutaneous, invasive and immune-mediated diseases. Although beta-lactams remain active, treatment alone has not controlled transmission, recurrent infection, rapid invasive progression or acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Control is further weakened by increased macrolide and clindamycin resistance, heterogeneous diagnostic access, asymptomatic carriage, crowded living conditions and unreliable continuity of secondary prophylaxis. These limitations have shifted the field from a predominantly treatment-centered approach toward the development of vaccines as a prevention strategy. Target selection is guided by virulence functions that are required for colonization, immune evasion and tissue injury. These include the M protein, group A carbohydrate (GAC), streptolysin O, Streptococcus pyogenes cell envelope protease (SpyCEP), Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and division protein (SpyAD), C5a peptidase and other conserved surface or secreted antigens. Current strategies include multivalent type-specific M-protein vaccines, conserved M-protein peptide vaccines, glycoconjugates, multicomponent non-M-protein formulations and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platforms. The clinical pipeline has recently broadened. Phase I studies have been completed for StreptAnova and MJ8VAX, whereas the J8-K4S2 and p*17-K4S2 clinical trial studies have been completed, with peer-reviewed results pending. The GSK four-component vaccine initiated phase I evaluation in 2025 and remained under clinical evaluation in 2026, whereas the VAX-A1 formulation entered a first-in-human phase I study in 2026. However, no licensed GAS vaccine is available. Progress remains constrained by uncertain correlates of protection, autoimmune safety requirements, geographical emm diversity, endpoint selection and the need for trials in high-burden populations. This narrative review therefore focuses on the disease problem, targetable virulence mechanisms, limits of antimicrobial control, current vaccine pipeline and interventions required to complement future vaccine use.

abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.
