abstract: Transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tDRs) are a class of functional small non-coding RNAs, many of which are induced by stress conditions and have been implicated in tissue injury and disease pathogenesis. However, their role in intestinal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains unclear. Using tDR sequencing, we identified that tDR-Glu-TTC was significantly upregulated in intestinal tissues, plasma, epithelial cells, and human clinical samples; and its levels positively correlated with the severity of intestinal injury. Functionally, tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal mucosal damage by activating TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis in intestinal epithelial cells. Mechanistically, tDR-Glu-TTC directly binds to and suppresses the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, impairing adenosine-to-inosine editing of autophagy-related transcripts (ATG18 and Lamp2). This inhibits autophagy, leading to the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, and the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS). The elevated ROS subsequently promotes TNF-α secretion, triggering TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis. Furthermore, increased ROS downregulates TRMT6/61A-dependent m¹A methylation of tRNA-Glu-TTC, increasing tDR-Glu-TTC biogenesis and forming a pathogenic positive feedback loop. Thus, therapeutic dual-target intervention using N-acetylcysteine combined with tDR-Glu-TTC-antagomir synergistically mitigated I/R-induced intestinal injury in vivo. In summary, our study unveiled a previously unrecognized mechanism by which tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal I/R injury via the ADAR1/autophagy/ROS/necroptosis signaling axis, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for combating intestinal I/R injury.

title: 1048 Targeting the early ovarian cancer antigen ORF1p with an mRNA-LNP vaccine for cancer interception

abstract: SIRPA delivers an anti-phagocytic "don't-eat-me" signal through its expression on macrophage membrane surface and promotes tumor progression via membrane-independent mechanism. However, current CD47- and SIRPA-targeting agents only disrupt cell-surface inhibitory signaling, highlighting the therapeutic potential of degrading SIRPA. Here, we identified that E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM2 interacted with SIRPA in vitro. Clinically, elevated TRIM2 expression is associated with prolonged overall and progression-free survival in renal-cell carcinoma (RCC) patients. Mechanistically, TRIM2 catalyzes K48-linked poly-ubiquitination of SIRPA, promoting its proteasomal degradation and reducing SIRPA protein levels. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of TRIM2 in macrophages upregulated SIRPA, significantly impairing phagocytosis of tumor cells. TRIM2 deficiency also promoted tumor growth by increasing intratumoral infiltration of M2-type macrophage, reducing accumulation of anti-tumor M1-like and antigen-presenting macrophages, and impairing effector CD8+ T-cell recruitment. Importantly, combined TRIM2 overexpression and PD-L1 blockade synergistically enhance anti-tumor immunity. Together, these results suggest that targeting TRIM2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy against RCC by degrading SIRPA in macrophage and provide a roadmap for clinical application.

title: TRIM2 facilitates macrophage mediated anti-tumor immunity in renal cell carcinoma through enhancing SIRPA ubiquitination and degradation.

abstract: Cellular senescence is accompanied by profound lysosomal alterations, yet whether lysosome-associated factors actively drive aging remains unclear. Through a focused CRISPR/Cas9 screen in human mesenchymal progenitor cells (hMPCs), we identified N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase subunits alpha and beta (GNPTAB), an enzyme responsible for lysosomal hydrolase targeting, as a positive regulator of cellular senescence. Genetic ablation of GNPTAB attenuated senescence, whereas its overexpression accelerated senescence. This pro-senescent function occurred independently of GNPTAB's canonical enzymatic role. Instead, GNPTAB binds to the innate immune adaptor stimulator of interferon genes (STING) through an interface involving the critical residue E1119, leading to activation of STING and its downstream TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), as well as pro-inflammatory gene expression. A STING-binding-deficient GNPTAB mutant (E1119A) preserved canonical lysosomal functions but failed to induce senescence, while STING depletion abolished GNPTAB-driven senescence. Together, these findings uncover a new signaling pathway wherein GNPTAB engages STING to facilitate its activation, suggesting that the GNPTAB-STING interaction interface may serve as a potential therapeutic target for ameliorating age-related cellular dysfunction.

title: CRISPR screening identifies GNPTAB as a noncanonical STING activator driving cellular senescence.

abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder characterized by dysregulation of the intestinal immune system, in which functional abnormalities of phagocytes such as macrophages play a critical role in pathogenesis. Although conventional therapies such as anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) antibodies are widely used in clinical practice, they have limitations including low response rates and significant side effects, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In recent years, macrophage-directed immunotherapy has emerged as a cutting-edge approach for IBD treatment by reprogramming intestinal phagocytes to restore immune homeostasis. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on the M1/M2 polarization framework, this review integrates recent single-cell discoveries of novel macrophage subsets (e.g. SPP1+ and TREM2+ macrophages), systematically examines the crosstalk among signaling, epigenetic, and metabolic regulatory layers, and critically evaluates translational barriers from preclinical models to clinical application. By evaluating preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the potential and challenges of these strategies. Through in-depth analysis, this review aims to provide a theoretical basis for the development of more precise and effective immunotherapies for IBD and to point out future research directions. (Literature search: PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase; January 2000-December 2025.).

title: Macrophage-directed immunotherapy in Inflammatory bowel disease: advances in reprogramming intestinal phagocytes.

abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.
